### D-376 — Map-literal construction lands: grammar, AST, type checking, `NewMap` opcode (July 2026)

Area: Language syntax / Type system / Compiler / VM — map-literal construction
Supersedes: none
Superseded by: none
Refines: D-374, D-375

**Grammar and disambiguation.** `map` is an ordinary bindable identifier today —
absent from `TypeChecker`'s `_reservedIdentifiers` and not namespace-registered (D-370's
precedent for `int`/`float` was not extended to `map`) — so `map := 5` is legal and
`map < x` is a genuine relational comparison. D-375 named the disambiguation as this
increment's own design work; it is a new non-consuming lookahead, `LooksLikeMapLiteral()`,
mirroring `LooksLikeStructConstruction()`'s peek-only style: a pure index scan over
`_tokens[_pos...]` that never calls `Advance`/`Expect`/`Match`, wired into `ParsePrimary`'s
`Identifier` case. It triggers only when the consumed identifier's lexeme is exactly
`"map"` and the *next* token (before consuming) is `Less`; it then scans forward from the
`<`, tracking `<`/`>` depth over a token run of identifiers, commas and optional `[`/`]`
(for an array-typed value argument), succeeding only if the matching top-level `>` is
immediately followed by `{`. A failed check leaves `_pos` untouched — the lookahead
never consumes anything — so `map < x` falls straight through to today's
`IdentifierExpr` path unchanged. This closes two open questions D-375 itself raised: **no
rewind primitive was needed**, because nothing was ever consumed on the failed path
(D-375 speculated a "speculative lookahead with rewind" would be required; a pure
non-consuming scan removed the need for rewind entirely); and **named-type construction's
existing machinery could not be reused**, because that path is a `ParsePostfix` case gated
on `e is IdentifierExpr`, and `map<string, string>` never parses to an `IdentifierExpr` in
the first place — a dedicated `ParsePrimary`-level production was the only option.
**No `_allowStructLiteral` wiring was needed anywhere** (D-375 had assumed it "must apply
to map literals as well"): the trigger is anchored on `map` immediately followed by `<`, a
signal that never arises from a bare identifier before a header's block-opening `{`
(`if (cond) { }`, `while (cond) { }`, `for k, v in m { }`, `case x { }`). This was proven
with regression tests exercising each of those headers, plus a map literal used *as* a
`for...in` iterable (`for k, v in map<string,int>{"a":1} { }`) to confirm the literal's own
closing `}` is never mistaken for the loop body's `{`, rather than assumed from reasoning
alone.

The type-argument list is parsed by a new shared `ParseTypeArgumentList()`, factored out
of `ParseTypePrimary`'s existing generic-args block: the `Match(TokenKind.Less)` check
stays in `ParseTypePrimary`, and the shared helper begins immediately after `<` is
consumed, so the map-literal path (which `Expect`s `Less` unconditionally, since the
lookahead already confirmed it) and the ordinary type-annotation path share one production
and cannot drift. The literal body — `ParseMapLiteral`/`ParseMapEntry`/
`ParseMapEntryKey` — mirrors `ParseArrayLiteral`/`ParseAnonStructLiteral` almost
exactly: comma-separated entries, newlines skipped, a trailing comma permitted (D-375's
ratified rule, applied verbatim). A map-literal key must be a plain double-quoted string
with no interpolation. The lexer has no dedicated "plain string" token kind — even a
non-interpolated double-quoted string lexes as a `StringStart`/`StringPart`/`StringEnd`
run, never a bare "string literal" token — so the key is parsed via the existing
`ParseInterpolatedString()` and then required to have every part be a `StringTextPart`,
mirroring the constant-folding check `Compiler.cs`'s `EvalConstantExpr` already uses to
recognise a non-interpolated double-quoted string as a compile-time constant. A raw
(backtick) string, an identifier, or a genuinely interpolated string as the key is E2001
("expected string literal key").

**AST.** `MapLiteralExpr(Range, TypeArguments: TypeRef, Entries: IReadOnlyList<MapEntry>)`
and `MapEntry(Range, Key: string, Value: Expression)` (new files under
`Grob.Compiler/Ast/Expressions/`). `MapEntry.Key` stores the decoded key as a plain
string, not a node — mirroring `FieldInit`'s established convention for a
construction site's field name. `MapLiteralExpr.TypeArguments` is the literal's own
`map<K, V>` `TypeRef`, built directly from the parsed type-argument list (`Name: "map"`),
which is exactly the shape `ResolveMapValueDescriptor(TypeRef)` (D-374, entirely
unchanged) already consumes — reading `TypeArguments[1]` for `V` — so no adapter
or overload was needed. `AstVisitor.VisitMapLiteral` and an `AstWalker` override (visiting
each entry's `Value`) were added, mirroring `VisitArrayLiteral`/`VisitAnonStruct`'s
existing hooks.

**Type checking.** A new `_mapLiteralDescriptors` dictionary (`Dictionary<MapLiteralExpr,
MapTypeDescriptor>`, keyed by reference identity) mirrors `_arrayLiteralDescriptors`
exactly, populated by a new `VisitMapLiteral` from `ResolveMapValueDescriptor(node.
TypeArguments)`. `MapDescriptorOf` (D-374) gains a third arm —
`MapLiteralExpr literal => _mapLiteralDescriptors.GetValueOrDefault(literal)` —
alongside the identifier and grouping tiers it already had; D-374's own doc comment
("only the two tiers with a real producer today are handled") is updated to reflect
three. This closes D-374's own noted gap directly: a `:=`-inferred binding from a map
literal now carries a real `MapTypeDescriptor` (`ResolveBindingFull` already calls
`MapDescriptorOf(initExpr)` generically for any initialiser, so this required no change to
that call site), so `m := map<string, int>{"a": 1}` followed by `m["a"]` types `int?` and
`for k, v in m` binds `v` as `int`, exactly as a `map<string, int>`-annotated parameter
already did.

Each entry's value is visited unconditionally — even a duplicate key's own value, so
its identifiers resolve and the tree is fully annotated for later passes regardless —
and checked against `V` via a new `CheckMapEntryValue` helper. It is built from the same
primitives `CheckArrayElementArgument` uses (`TypesAreAssignable`, `ArrayElementAssignable`
for a nested `map<string, T[]>` value's element identity, `IsStructNominalMismatch` for a
nested named-struct value's nominal identity) but does not call that method directly —
a map entry has no `MemberAccessExpr` receiver to phrase the diagnostic's wording around,
which `CheckArrayElementArgument`'s signature requires. A mismatch is `ErrorCatalog.E0004`
(reused, never a new code, per this increment's brief). `K` (the key type argument) stays
unvalidated, unchanged from `ResolveMapValueDescriptor`'s existing, deliberate, documented
gap — not this increment's concern. A malformed `map<X>{...}` literal (fewer than two
type arguments) resolves no descriptor at all and stays permissive — no per-entry
value check runs, mirroring the array-literal analogue's own missing-descriptor
convention, and nothing crashes.

**Duplicate-key rule and its error code.** Iterating a literal's entries with a
`HashSet<string>(StringComparer.Ordinal)` of seen keys, shaped exactly like
`TypeChecker.Declarations.cs`'s E2208 duplicate-field-name check, a repeat key raises a
**new error code, E0016** ("duplicate key in map literal"). Confirmed against the live
registry immediately before allocating: `E0001`–`E0015` were in use, leaving `E0016`
free in the `E00xx` sub-block (matching the plan-time expectation exactly). None of the
three existing duplicate-entry codes fits: E0010 (duplicate named argument) is call-site
only, E2208 (duplicate field name) is `type`-declaration only, and E2213 (duplicate
`catch`) is exception-handling only — matching the E0014/E0015 precedent (a distinct,
more-actionable construction-site code earns its own number rather than an ill-fitting
fold). Registered in three-location lockstep in `grob-error-codes.md` (summary index row,
full entry citing this decision, footer total 118 → 119) and in `ErrorCatalog`
(`Grob.Core`); the D-316 consistency gate (`Grob.Consistency.Tests`) re-verified green at
119. A gold-master pair was added at `docs/errors/examples/duplicate-key-map-literal/`.

**Codegen and the `NewMap` opcode.** The archived kickoff prompt's own working assumption
was that construction needed no new opcode; this did not hold. `SetIndex` (the VM's
existing map-receiver arm) only mutates a map that already exists — there is no way to
allocate a fresh, empty `GrobMap` from bytecode without one. A genuine new allocation
primitive was required, not merely a mutation one, so `OpCode.NewMap` was added following
`adding-an-opcode`. Appended after `Import` (the enum's previous last case) in a new "Map
operations" section — appended, not inserted, so no existing opcode's implicit byte
value shifts, the identical precedent this file's own header comment already documents for
`LessDate`/`GreaterDate`/`EqualDate` (D-354/D-357). Operand: a 1-byte entry count; the VM
pops `2×count` values as source-ordered `(key: string, value)` pairs and pushes a new
`GrobMap`, mirroring `NewAnonStruct`'s name/value-pair stack-layout convention exactly. VM
dispatch was added in `VirtualMachine.cs` near `NewAnonStruct` for readability (the enum's
own physical position does not need to match); it was also wired into the "1-byte operand"
`ip`-advance table in the same file, the `Disassembler.cs` dispatch switch
(`ByteOperandInstruction`), and `DisassemblerTests`' per-opcode exhaustiveness width table
— three sites the archived kickoff prompt's file list did not name individually, found
by running the full `Grob.Vm.Tests` suite (the disassembler's own exhaustive
`Enum.GetValues<OpCode>()` theory fails immediately for an unhandled opcode) rather than
assumed complete from the prompt's shorter list. A runtime duplicate key is not separately
rejected — `GrobMap.Set`'s existing last-write-wins semantics apply at the VM layer,
matching the compile-time diagnostic's role of catching the mistake at the earliest
possible point rather than the VM re-deriving the same check. Compiler emission
(`Compiler.Expressions.cs`) — a new `VisitMapLiteral` — mirrors `VisitAnonStruct`
verbatim: per entry, a key-string constant plus `OpCode.Constant`, then the value
expression; finished with `OpCode.NewMap` and `ToByteOperand(node.Entries.Count, "map
literal entry count")`, the same bounds-check helper `VisitArrayLiteral` already uses,
reused rather than duplicated.

**Corpus.** D-375's separator ratification was applied across five files, not the three
D-375 itself named, plus the wiki page: `grob-type-registry.md` (the separator-rules
block, the Construction example, and the build-status note, now citing this decision
rather than D-374's "not yet built" framing); `grob-language-fundamentals.md` (a new "Map
literals" subsection under §8 "Literals" — previously covering only
Integer/Float/String/Bool/Nil/Array, a gap `grob-grammar-audit.md`'s finding G1 named as a
contributing cause of the documented-but-unbuilt confusion); `grob-sample-scripts.md`
(Script 11's four-entry `tags` literal, newline-separated to comma-separated);
`grob-stdlib-reference.md` (two sites D-375 did not name: an `http.get()` inline
single-entry literal, which needed no separator change since it has only one entry, and a
`guid`-module single-entry example, given a trailing comma for convention consistency even
though it too has only one entry); and `docs/wiki/Type-Registry/map.md` (its "Not yet
built (D-374)" Construction callout, now reading built and citing this decision, plus its
own Construction example updated to commas). The §14/G1 citation naming "line-1321" as
needing a comma fix was re-verified rather than trusted: no map example exists in §14
("Line Continuation") at all; the actual comma-separated, trailing-comma-bearing example
lives in §16 ("Trailing Commas"), and it was already correct at plan time — no
content change was needed there beyond confirming this, closing the citation-hygiene gap
D-375/G1 both carried forward.

**Scope.** Map query and mutation members (`length`/`isEmpty`/`keys`/`values`/`get`/`set`/
`remove`/`clear`) remain unbuilt, unchanged from D-374's own stated deferral to a C0b-2
follow-on increment — this increment is construction only, exactly as scoped.

One new opcode, `OpCode.NewMap` (see above). One new error code, E0016; count 118 → 119.

Full detail: D-375 (the separator ratification this increment implements against), D-374
(the `MapTypeDescriptor` substrate this increment's third tier extends), D-137 (map first
introduced as a first-class built-in), D-300 (parser error-recovery model the map-literal
grammar's failure paths reuse unchanged), D-371 and D-373 (the array-literal/array-member
precedents this increment's type-checking and codegen shape mirror throughout),
`grob-grammar-audit.md` (finding G1, the documented-but-unbuilt map-literal gap this
increment closes).

### D-377 — Map query member surface lands: length/isEmpty/keys/values/get/contains (Sprint 9 Increment C0b-2a) (July 2026)

Area: Type system / Compiler / VM — map query member surface
Supersedes: none
Superseded by: none
Refines: D-374, D-376

Builds the six non-mutating `map<K, V>` members `grob-type-registry.md` had advertised
since before D-374: `length`/`isEmpty`/`keys`/`values` (properties) and `get(key)`/
`contains(key)` (methods) — the last collection-surface finding from the
advertised-vs-built audit (`grob-advertised-vs-built-audit.md`, finding B2) still open.
`set`/`remove`/`clear` and their `readonly` mutation rejection are the separate increment
C0b-2b, mirroring the C0a-1/C0a-2 split D-371/D-373 already established for arrays.
Confirmed at plan time by direct read: `TypeChecker.Expressions.cs` had no `GrobType.Map`
arm anywhere — neither in `VisitMemberAccess` (property form) nor `ResolveMemberAccessCall`
(call form) — despite the substrate (`MapTypeDescriptor`, `MapDescriptorOf`,
`ResolveMapValueDescriptor`, the `m[k] → V?` indexer, `for k, v in m`, map literals) being
complete since D-374/D-376. This increment mirrors D-371's array query-member dispatch
shape exactly — no third pattern was invented.

**Dispatch.** `ResolveMapPropertyAccess` (new) is called from `VisitMemberAccess` alongside
the pre-existing array arm — both were folded into one guard-clause helper,
`ResolveCollectionPropertyAccess`, purely to keep `VisitMemberAccess` under the S3776
cognitive-complexity bar (16 → under 15 after the extraction); no behaviour change from the
extraction itself. `length`/`isEmpty` resolve directly (no descriptor needed, mirroring
array's identical latitude). `IsMapMethod`/`ValidateMapMethodCall` (new) are called from
`ResolveMemberAccessCall` directly alongside the array method arm, for `get`/`contains`.

**The `keys`/`values` descriptor composition — the one genuinely new piece.** `keys`/
`values` return `GrobType.Array` but must carry a _populated_ `ArrayTypeDescriptor` so a
chained access (`m.keys.first()`, `m.values.contains(x)`) resolves rather than degrading to
`Unknown` — proven by a load-bearing test asserting `m.keys.first()` types `string?` and
`m.values.contains(2)` types `bool` on a real `map<string, int>` literal (D-376), plus a
`map<string, int[]>` case whose `.values.first()` types `int[]?`, proving the nested
`ArrayTypeDescriptor`/`MapTypeDescriptor` composition (not just the flat kind) survives.
This required a genuinely new descriptor-carriage tier: `ArrayDescriptorOf` (`TypeChecker.cs`)
previously had no `MemberAccessExpr` case at all — every property access before now
resolved to a non-array type (`length`/`isEmpty`/primitive scalars/struct fields), so no
property access had ever needed to carry an element descriptor forward. A new
`_memberAccessArrayDescriptors: Dictionary<MemberAccessExpr, ArrayTypeDescriptor>` (keyed by
reference identity, mirroring every other descriptor side-channel in the file) is populated
by `ResolveMapPropertyAccess` and consulted by a new `ArrayDescriptorOf` arm. `keys`'s
descriptor is always `new ArrayTypeDescriptor(GrobType.String)` (`K` is fixed `string` in
v1); `values`'s is composed directly from the receiver's `MapTypeDescriptor`
(`ValueKind`/`ValueNamedTypeName`/`ValueArrayDescriptor`), which is what makes the nested
`int[][]` case above compose correctly with no special-casing.

**`get`/indexer agreement.** The registry documents `[key]` as "sugar for `get(key)`";
D-374 already types `m[k]` as `V?`. Rather than merge the two AST shapes (`IndexExpr` and
`CallExpr` have different surrounding arity/argument-check machinery, so a full
visitor-level merge was not the available seam), the one-line type derivation
(`ToNullable(descriptor?.ValueKind ?? Unknown)`) was factored into a shared
`MapValueResultType(MapTypeDescriptor?)` helper, called from both `VisitIndex` and
`ValidateMapMethodCall`'s `get` case — proven never to drift rather than duplicated. At the
VM layer the same sharing seam holds: `MapNatives.Get` and `OpCode.GetIndex`'s existing map
arm both call `GrobMap.TryGetValue` — the same runtime lookup backs `m[k]` and `m.get(k)`,
even though they remain two separate opcodes/call shapes (the array precedent never merges
indexer and method dispatch either). A test proves `m.get(k)` and `m[k]` agree on type and
value for both a present and an absent key.

**`contains` is deliberately key-membership.** Unlike the array's `contains(v: T)` (value
membership, D-371), the map's `contains(key: K)` asks whether the _key_ is present — same
member name, different subject, on two collection types. Recorded here as deliberate, per
the registry's own wording, with a test contrasting `map.contains(k)` against
`map.values.contains(v)` on the same underlying data so the asymmetry cannot be "corrected"
by mistake later.

**Runtime.** `GrobMap` (`Grob.Core`) gains one new member, `InsertionOrderValues`, mirroring
the pre-existing `InsertionOrderKeys` exactly (`OrderedDictionary<K,V>.Values` is already
order-preserving and already `IReadOnlyList<V>`) — reused, not reimplemented; insertion
order for both `keys` and `values` comes from the one ordered backing store, proven to
survive the indexer-write mutation path (`m["z"] = 1; m["a"] = 2`) as well as literal
construction. `VirtualMachine.cs`'s `OpCode.GetProperty` map branch — previously built only
for the internal `for k, v in m` lowering's own `EmitGetProperty("keys", ...)` call, never
reachable from user-written `.keys` since no checker arm existed to type-check it — is
extended to a full mirror of the array branch: `length`/`isEmpty`/`values` resolve inline,
`get`/`contains` resolve via a new `MapNatives.cs` (`Grob.Vm`), mirroring `ArrayNatives.cs`'s
factory shape. No new opcode — `GetProperty` and `Call` were already sufficient, confirmed
before writing any VM code (the same confirmation D-371 made for arrays). No compiler
(`Compiler.Expressions.cs`) change at all: property access and method calls on a map
receiver already emit generically, exactly as they do for arrays — a fact proven by the
bytecode-shape test suite passing with zero compiler-side edits.

**`CompilerNullableTests` re-anchored a third time — and this one is terminal.** The
permissive-`Unknown` property-access fall-through this suite's `PlainDot_DoesNotEmitIsNilOrJumps`
has exercised since Sprint 3 moved `int` → `array` (D-369) → `map` (D-371) → now
function-typed (`fn(...): R`, `GrobType.Function`). Walking every `GrobType` value against
`VisitMemberAccess`'s dispatch chain directly (not assumed): every primitive, nullable
variant, struct/anon-struct, array and now map receiver is intercepted before the bottom
fall-through; `Nil` and `Error` are intercepted even earlier (cascade suppression / a
degenerate case); `Function` is the sole survivor. Unlike `int`/`array`/`map` — each
"not yet built" and each eventually registered — `Function`'s memberless status is a
**locked** design decision: `grob-type-registry.md` states permanently, "Members. None. A
function type has no properties, no methods and no constructor syntax." No future increment
is going to register function members and force a fourth move, so this re-anchor is
terminal — filed here as the property-access analogue of D-362's enumerated
arithmetic-operand permissive-`Unknown` sources, a closed finding rather than a defect (the
fall-through's continued existence is required — it is what keeps `?.`-chain/`Unknown`-target
access permissive — its reachability for a _registered, non-nullable_ type is what closed).

No new opcode. No new error code — key-argument mismatches reuse `E0004`, arity reuses
`E0003`, the unrecognised-member reuses `E1002`; count stays **119**.

Full detail: D-374 (the `MapTypeDescriptor` substrate this increment builds on), D-376 (map
literals, the real-source construction every new test uses), D-371 and D-373 (the array
query/mutating-member precedents this increment's dispatch and native-factory shape mirror
throughout), D-350 (the map for-in lowering whose internal `GetProperty("keys", ...)` call
this increment's checker arm finally makes independently reachable from user source), D-362
(the arithmetic-operand permissive-`Unknown` catalogue this increment's property-access
finding parallels), `grob-advertised-vs-built-audit.md` (finding B2, closed for the query
half; the mutating half stays open for C0b-2b).

### D-378 — Map mutating member surface lands: set/remove/clear (Sprint 9 Increment C0b-2b) (July 2026)

Area: Type system / Compiler / VM — map mutating member surface
Supersedes: none
Superseded by: none
Refines: D-377, D-376, D-374, D-373, D-372

Builds the three in-place-mutating `map<K, V>` members D-377 deferred — `set(key: K,
value: V)`, `remove(key: K)`, `clear()` — completing the `map<K, V>` surface D-374/D-376/
D-377 began, and with it the collection surface as a whole: arrays (D-371/D-373), maps
(D-374/D-376/D-377/D-378), strings (D-363/D-365), numerics (D-369/D-370). Closes the
mutating half of the advertised-vs-built audit's finding B2 (`grob-advertised-vs-built-audit.md`),
the last open item of the collection-surface work. Mirrors D-373's array mutating-member
increment exactly — no new pattern was invented; confirmed at plan time by direct read of
`ValidateArrayMutatingMethodCall`, `FindReadonlyRoot`, `ArrayNatives.cs` and `GrobMap.cs`
before writing any code.

**Dispatch.** `IsMapMethod` (`TypeChecker.Expressions.cs`) extended to recognise `set`/
`remove`/`clear` alongside the pre-existing `get`/`contains`. A new
`ValidateMapMutatingMethodCall`, dispatched from `ValidateMapMethodCall`'s switch, mirrors
`ValidateArrayMutatingMethodCall` line for line: `FindReadonlyRoot(memberAccess.Target)`
(`TypeChecker.Statements.cs`) is called first and, if the receiver chain roots in a
`readonly` binding, emits **E0204** without early-returning — so an independent arity
(E0003, via the existing `MemberArgCountMatches`) or argument-type (E0004) diagnostic is
still collected alongside it, proven by a test asserting both fire together. Confirmed
`FindReadonlyRoot` needed no change at all: it already walks arbitrary
`MemberAccessExpr`/`IndexExpr` nesting by AST shape, not by receiver type, so
`ro.items.set(...)` on a map-valued struct field was already covered — pinned by a test
mirroring D-373's chained-struct-field case.

**Value/key type checking — the reuse judgement call.** `remove`'s and `set`'s key
argument reuse `CheckMapKeyArgument` (D-377) verbatim — already call-site shaped, no
change needed. `set`'s value argument needed a new helper, `CheckMapValueArgument`: D-376's
`CheckMapEntryValue` is shaped for a `MapEntry` (a literal's key/value pair) and phrases
its diagnostic around the entry's key, not a call argument, so it could not be called
directly from a method-call site — the same reason D-376 itself gives for not reusing
`CheckArrayElementArgument` verbatim. `CheckMapValueArgument` takes
`CheckArrayElementArgument`'s call-site shape (`MemberAccessExpr`, `GrobType`,
`Expression`, descriptor), and the compatibility rules themselves — `TypesAreAssignable`
plus the array-element and struct-nominal-mismatch arms — were extracted out of
`CheckMapEntryValue` into a shared `IsMapValueCompatible` predicate that both methods call,
so the map-literal value check and the `set` value check are literally the same check and
cannot diverge in what they accept; only the diagnostic wording differs. (The extraction
was made under PR #166 review: the increment as first written copy-pasted the rules into
both methods, which left the never-diverge property a convention rather than a guarantee.)
A mismatch is
`E0004`, never a new code; no descriptor available stays permissive, matching every other
element/value check in the file.

**The `set`/`SetIndex` write-path seam — confirmed shared, not duplicated.** `GrobMap.Set`
(already used by `OpCode.SetIndex`'s map arm since D-350) is the single write path;
`MapNatives.Set` calls it directly rather than re-implementing the assignment, so `m.set(k,
v)` and `m[k] = v` can never drift — proven by a test asserting the two produce identical
state (value and insertion order) for both a new and an existing key.

**Insertion order — confirmed, not reimplemented.** `GrobMap` is backed by
`OrderedDictionary<string, GrobValue>`; its indexer-set contract (overwriting an existing
key preserves position, inserting a new key appends) is inherited for free through
`GrobMap.Set` — no bookkeeping was added. The load-bearing ordering test (D-377's own
guarantee, which `set` must not violate) locks both directions: a new key appears last in
`keys`, an overwritten key's position is unchanged, and `values` stays index-aligned with
`keys` throughout.

**`remove`'s no-op — confirmed deliberate, the opposite of the array.** `GrobMap` gains
`Remove(string key)` and `Clear()`, thin unguarded wrappers mirroring `GrobArray`'s
`RemoveAt`/`Clear` precedent. Unlike the array's bounds-checked, `IndexError`-throwing
`remove(index)` (D-373), the map's `remove(key)` is a no-op when the key is absent — per
`grob-type-registry.md`'s own documented contract — with no `NativeFaultException` path at
all. Recorded here as a deliberate asymmetry, alongside D-377's `contains` key- versus
value-membership asymmetry, so neither gets "corrected" by a future increment. `MapNatives.cs`
gains `Set`/`Remove`/`Clear`, mirroring `ArrayNatives.cs`'s factory shape exactly — none of
the three takes a function argument, so the `VmInvoker` parameter stays unused, matching
`get`/`contains`'s existing precedent (CodeRabbit review, PR #165). No new opcode —
`GetProperty`/`Call` were already sufficient, confirmed before writing any VM code, exactly
as D-377 confirmed for the query half.

**`for k, v in m` during mutation — investigated, found milder than the array case,
reported not fixed.** `Compiler.ControlFlow.cs`'s `EmitMapForIn` materialises the map's
`keys` array **once** into a synthetic local before the loop starts, then walks a counter
against `keys.length` — unlike `EmitArrayForIn`, which re-reads `arr.length` fresh every
iteration (D-373's known finding). Consequence, confirmed by reading the bytecode shape (no
live C# `IEnumerator` is ever held across Grob bytecode, so no "collection modified during
enumeration" exception is possible here): the loop's iteration count is fixed at entry — a
mutating loop body cannot grow or shrink how many times the loop runs, unlike the array's
visibly shifting bound — but a key removed (or every key, after `clear()`) mid-loop is
still visited, and its `v = m[k]` read degrades to `nil` (permissive, matching `get`'s
existing miss behaviour) rather than throwing or skipping. Pinned by an integration test
exercising exactly this shape. Logged here for the pending correctness batch, alongside
D-373's array for-in-bound finding and D-372's `readonly` binding-scope gap — not fixed in
this branch, per this increment's own scope boundary.

**Aliasing — D-372's ratification, pinned directly.** `a := map<...>{...}; b := a;
b.set(k, v)` leaves `a`'s state mutated too, tested at the VM layer (`Assert.Same` on the
two aliased `GrobMap` references) and end to end (through a second binding and through a
function parameter, mirroring D-373's array aliasing tests exactly). The known
binding-scoped `readonly` gap D-372 already recorded (a `readonly` map aliased to a mutable
binding is mutable through that alias) is not fixed here — matching the array precedent,
no new decision needed to reproduce it for maps.

No new opcode. No new error code — `readonly` rejection reuses `E0204`, argument-type
mismatches reuse `E0004`, arity reuses `E0003`; count stays **119**.

Full detail: D-377 (the query-member dispatch and native-factory shape this increment
extends), D-376 (`CheckMapEntryValue`, whose compatibility logic is now the shared
`IsMapValueCompatible` predicate `CheckMapValueArgument` also calls), D-374 (`MapTypeDescriptor`, consulted by the new value-argument check), D-373 (the
array mutating-member precedent this increment mirrors throughout, including the E0204
method-call-site pattern and the for-in-during-mutation finding's shape), D-372 (the
reference-semantics/aliasing ratification this increment's aliasing tests pin for maps),
D-350 (`GrobMap.Set`/`SetIndex`, the write path this increment's `set` shares),
D-291 (E0204's origin), `grob-advertised-vs-built-audit.md` (finding B2, now fully closed).

### D-379 — `for...in` snapshots its bound at loop entry, for every collection type (July 2026)

Area: Language semantics / Compiler — iteration
Supersedes: none
Superseded by: none
Refines: D-373, D-378

**The inconsistency.** Two increments independently investigated what happens when a `for...in`
loop body mutates the collection it is iterating, and found two different answers:

- **Arrays (D-373).** `EmitArrayForIn` re-reads the loop bound through a fresh
  `GetProperty("length")` call on **every iteration** rather than capturing it once. A body that
  calls `append` or `insert` on the array it iterates changes the loop's own bound mid-flight —
  and an unconditional `append` iterates unboundedly.
- **Maps (D-378).** `EmitMapForIn` materialises the map's `keys` array **once** into a synthetic
  local before the loop starts, then walks a counter against that array's fixed length. The
  iteration count is therefore fixed at entry; a body calling `set`, `remove` or `clear` cannot
  change how many times the loop runs.

Neither behaviour was chosen. Both fell out of separate implementations written months apart, and
each was found by reading bytecode during an unrelated increment's plan-mode. **The inconsistency
is the finding** — more than either behaviour considered alone. A language whose identity is
"readable by any C# or Go developer without prior knowledge" cannot have two collection types
that iterate by different rules, discovered only by experiment.

**The decision.** `for...in` **snapshots its bound at loop entry, for every collection type.**
Arrays align to maps: `EmitArrayForIn` captures the length once into a synthetic local before the
loop and walks a counter against it, exactly as `EmitMapForIn` already does with `keys`. Maps are
unchanged — they already implement the ratified behaviour.

**Why snapshot.**

- **Go's precedent, which Grob's syntax already borrows.** Go's `range` evaluates its range
  expression once before the loop begins; the length of a slice is captured, not re-read. Grob's
  `for...in` is the same shape and should carry the same guarantee.
- **A fixed count cannot iterate unboundedly.** The array's live bound turns an unconditional
  `append` inside a loop body into a hang — the worst failure mode available, because it produces
  no diagnostic at all. That is the wrong default for a scripting language whose users are
  sysadmins running things in production.
- **One rule beats two.** Consistency across collection types is worth more than either
  behaviour's local merits.

**What this does *not* change.** Mutation during iteration remains **permitted**. This decision
fixes the iteration *count*; it does not forbid the mutation, add a guard, or introduce a
diagnostic. The consequences D-378 confirmed for maps therefore stand and now apply uniformly:

- A key removed (or every key, after `clear()`) mid-loop is **still visited**, and its `v = m[k]`
  read degrades to `nil` — permissive, matching `get`'s existing miss behaviour.
- An element appended to an array mid-loop is **not visited** on that pass.

Both are documented consequences of a snapshot, not defects.

**Rejected alternatives.**

- **Align maps to arrays (live bound everywhere).** Rejected: a live bound admits unbounded
  iteration, and re-reading is the more surprising of the two directions for a reader coming from
  Go or C#.
- **Throw on mutation during iteration**, the C# `InvalidOperationException` / Python
  dict-changed-size model. Rejected for v1: it requires runtime modification tracking on every
  collection, plus a new error code, and there is nothing to invalidate — D-378 confirmed by
  reading the emitted bytecode that no live C# `IEnumerator` is ever held across Grob bytecode.
  The cost is a new subsystem; the benefit over a predictable snapshot is small. Reconsider
  post-v1 if real scripts show the permissive behaviour causing silent bugs.

**Implementation consequence — this changes shipped behaviour.** Arrays iterate differently after
this lands. The implementing increment must enumerate every test and validation script whose
behaviour changes and report the list before editing, per the standing rule that a test may be
updated to assert new correct behaviour but never weakened to accommodate a change.

No new opcode. No new error code; count unchanged at **119**.

Full detail: D-373 (the array live-bound finding), D-378 (the map snapshot behaviour and the
bytecode-level confirmation that no enumerator crosses the boundary),
`grob-language-fundamentals.md`'s `for...in` section, which should state the snapshot guarantee
explicitly once the increment lands.

### D-380 — Type-checker tightening: void-in-arithmetic and unrecognised method calls (July 2026)

Area: Compiler — type checking / bytecode emission
Supersedes: none
Superseded by: none
Refines: D-362, D-373

**The decision.** Closes two permissive-`Unknown` findings from the correctness batch —
D-362 (a `void`-returning call used as an arithmetic operand) and D-373 (an unrecognised
method name on a receiver whose type is known) — mirroring D-377's property-path tightening
onto the method-call path rather than inventing a second pattern.

**Empirical sweep first: the scope was narrower than the kickoff prompt assumed.** Several
of D-373's named gaps were already closed incidentally by later increments before this one
started: `string`/`int`/`float`/`bool` method calls already raise `E1002` on an unrecognised
name via `PrimitiveMemberRegistry` (D-369 registered `int`/`float`/`bool` *after* D-373 was
logged; D-363 registered `string` earlier still), and a registered named-type's method calls
already raise `E1002` (D-356). The only receivers still open for D-373's method-call finding
were **array and map** — the same shape D-374 already closed for D-362's map-element
arithmetic source before this increment began.

**Array/map unrecognised method call → E1002, reusing dead code rather than adding a new
branch.** `ValidateArrayMethodCall`/`ValidateMapMethodCall` already contained a `switch` with
a `default: return GrobType.Unknown;` arm — unreachable, because the outer dispatch gate
(`receiverType == GrobType.Array && IsArrayMethod(...)`, mirrored for `Map`) filtered an
unrecognised name out before the switch ever saw it. The fix drops the `IsArrayMethod`/
`IsMapMethod` name-gate (each had exactly one caller; both helpers, now unused, are deleted
rather than left dead) so every `Array`/`Map`-receiver call reaches the switch regardless of
name, and turns the two `default` arms into `E1002`, reusing `ResolveArrayPropertyAccess`'s/
`ResolveMapPropertyAccess`'s exact message shape (`Type 'T[]' has no member '{name}'.` /
`Type 'map<string, V>' has no member '{name}'.`). `Unknown`-typed receivers (untyped lambda
parameters — always `Unknown` in v1, `VisitLambda` registers every parameter that way
unconditionally, with no contextual inference) and `?.` chains on a nullable receiver stay
permissive for free: neither ever matches the exact `receiverType == GrobType.Array`/
`GrobType.Map` check, since a nullable array/map is its own distinct `GrobType` variant — no
dedicated nullable guard was needed on this path, unlike the property path's generic one.

**Void-in-arithmetic → E0002, via a new `CallExpr.IsVoidReturn` flag.** `GrobType` has no
`Void` variant — void is represented as `GrobType.Unknown` by deliberate convention — so type
alone cannot distinguish a genuinely void call from the other permissive-`Unknown` operand
sources (an untyped lambda-parameter identifier, an Unknown-receiver-field
`MemberAccessExpr`). A new settable `CallExpr.IsVoidReturn` bool (mirroring the
`ResolvedReturnType`/`ResolvedPrimitiveNativeName` annotation convention D-362 established on
the same node — not a new AST node, not grammar growth) is set `true` at exactly the three
places that resolve void: `ValidateArrayMethodCall`'s `each` case, and the tails of
`ValidateArrayMutatingMethodCall`/`ValidateMapMutatingMethodCall` — covering `each`/`append`/
`insert`/`remove`/`clear`/`set`. `ResolveArithmetic` gains a guard-clause helper,
`RejectVoidArithmeticOperand` (extracted to keep the method's cognitive complexity under the
S3776 bar), checked ahead of the existing `Unknown` pass-through: either operand being a void
`CallExpr` now raises `E0002` with the same message template the pre-existing Struct/Function
combinatorial reject uses, substituting the literal string `"void"` for the void side (there
is no real type name to print) — e.g. `arr.each(fn) + 1` now reports `Operator '+' cannot be
applied to types 'void' and 'int'.` A void call as a bare statement is unaffected — proven by
a dedicated regression test — this only rejects the arithmetic-operand position.
`EmitArithmetic`'s belt-and-braces defensive guard (`ThrowIfStructOrLambdaOperand`, renamed
`ThrowIfStructLambdaOrVoidOperand`) is extended with the same `IsVoidReturn` check, mirroring
the existing Struct/Lambda precedent exactly.

**Grouping is unwrapped on both checks (CodeRabbit review, PR #167).** The first cut matched a
bare `CallExpr` only. `GroupingExpr` is a real node the parser emits, so `(arr.each(f)) + 1`
presented the void call wrapped, walked past the reject into the permissive `Unknown`
pass-through, and still crashed the VM with the exact `GrobValue kind mismatch: expected Int,
actual Nil` internal error this entry exists to eliminate — the unparenthesised form was fixed
while its parenthesised twin was not. Both `RejectVoidArithmeticOperand` and
`ThrowIfStructLambdaOrVoidOperand` now unwrap `GroupingExpr` **recursively** (`while`, not a
single `if`, so `((...)) + 1` rejects identically), reusing the same unwrap
`ExpressionDescriptor`/`ArrayDescriptorOf`/`CheckCondition` already perform rather than
inventing a parallel one. The emission-side guard is unwrapped too, so it stays a genuine
backstop instead of a shape-sensitive one. Regressions cover the grouped, nested-grouped,
right-operand and grouped-map-mutating (`(m.set(k, v)) + 1`) forms, plus an over-reject
control — `(arr.length) + 1` still compiles and evaluates — since the unwrap must not widen
the reject beyond void calls.

**D-362's permissive-`Unknown` catalogue, corrected, not just reduced.** The kickoff prompt
assumed the live count was "two now, one after" (void plus the Unknown-receiver field). The
actual code comment (`Compiler.Expressions.cs`) named **three** active sources — the untyped
lambda-parameter identifier, the Unknown-receiver-field `MemberAccessExpr` (D-360), and the
void-returning `CallExpr` (D-362) — plus a fourth, already-closed source (a map element with a
known value type, closed by D-374, but mis-cited in the comment as "D-359"; D-359 is actually
"index-target compound assignment and increment/decrement", unrelated). Closing the void
source here reduces the live count to **two** (the lambda-parameter identifier and the
Unknown-receiver-field `MemberAccessExpr`), not one — the comment is rewritten to name exactly
those two, citing this entry for the third source's closure, with the D-359→D-374 citation
corrected in the same edit.

**Empirical before/after, confirmed via the CLI.** `arr.each(fn) + 1`, `arr.garbage()` and
`m.garbage()` previously type-checked cleanly and crashed the VM at runtime — an internal
"opcode GetProperty ... not yet implemented" / "GrobValue kind mismatch" error — a worse
failure mode than a compile error, since it produces no diagnostic pointing at the actual
mistake. All three now report `E0002`/`E1002` at compile time.

**New findings surfaced during this increment, not fixed here** (each is its own, smaller gap
than the ones this increment closes; reported per the standing "surface, don't silently
resolve" rule):

- The method-call path has no generic nullable guard mirroring `VisitMemberAccess`'s — a
  non-optional `.` on a nullable array/primitive/ordinary-struct receiver doesn't get the
  `E0101` nil-dereference diagnostic the property path gives it, unlike a registered named
  type's nullable receiver, which already does (a narrower, pre-existing special case).
- An ordinary user `type` struct's method call is permissive regardless of name — v1 gives
  structs no method surface at all, unlike the property path's `ResolveStructFieldAccess`,
  which already raises `E1002` for an unrecognised field. `AnonStruct`/`NullableAnonStruct`
  method calls are the same.
- No `Error`-receiver cascade-suppression arm exists on the call path (unlike
  `VisitMemberAccess:1294`), so a call on an already-errored receiver resolves `Unknown`
  rather than `Error`.
- Found during the CLI spot-check: `?.` short-circuiting is wired at the VM level for
  property access but **not** for method calls — `xs?.first()` on a nil `int[]?` crashes with
  "Call target is not a function (kind: Nil)" even though `first` is a recognised method,
  proving the gap is a runtime dispatch omission, orthogonal to this increment's
  type-checker-only change (confirmed by testing a *recognised* method name via `?.`, which
  crashes identically).

**Tests.** One existing test updated for the breaking change —
`CompilerCallOperandTypingTests.VoidReturningCallAsOperand_ArrayEach_StillCompilesUnderIntAssumption`
→ `..._ReportsE0002`, now asserting the `E0002` diagnostic instead of a clean compile — the
only breaking-change hit found in a full corpus sweep of `tests/`, `docs/errors/examples/` and
every `.grob` fixture (no gold master, validation script, or `Grob.Integration.Tests` case
combines a void call with arithmetic or exercises `arr.garbage()`/`m.garbage()`). New tests:
the array/map unrecognised-method-call `E1002` cases and their required-permissive survivors
(an untyped lambda parameter, `?.` on a nullable receiver); six void-in-arithmetic `E0002`
cases (`+`/`-`/`*`/`/`/`%`, both operand positions, plus the array-append and map-set mutating
sources); a bare-void-statement-still-compiles regression; and `float`/`bool`
unrecognised-method-call `E1002` cases that were missing alongside the pre-existing `string`/
`int` ones in `TypeCheckerPrimitiveMemberTests.cs`.

No new opcode. No new error code — `E0002` and `E1002` both existed already; count stays
**119**.

Full detail: D-362 (the original void-in-arithmetic finding), D-373 (the original
unrecognised-method finding), D-377 (the property-path tightening this mirrors), D-374 (the
map-element arithmetic source it closed, and the source of the corrected citation above),
D-369 (registered `int`/`float`/`bool` method surfaces, closing part of D-373 incidentally),
D-363 (registered the `string` method surface), D-356 (registered named-type method
dispatch).

### D-381 — `print`/`exit` misuse rejected at compile time, not a runtime crash (July 2026)

Area: Compiler — type checking
Supersedes: none
Superseded by: none
Refines: none

**The decision.** `print`/`exit` are opcode-only sugar — `Compiler.Statements.cs`'s
`VisitExpressionStmt` emits the dedicated `Print`/`Exit` opcodes only for the exact
bare-statement shape it recognises structurally (the right name, the right arity), and
neither builtin has any other runtime representation: unlike `input()` (a genuine
global-backed native, callable from any position), there is no global ever registered
for `print`/`exit`. Before this entry the type checker validated neither the shape nor
the arity, so every other use — a malformed arity even in statement position
(`print()`, `print("a", "b")`), a call whose result is consumed (`y := print("x")`,
`1 + print(x)`), or a bare reference with no call at all (`y := print`) — type-checked
permissively and fell through to a generic global lookup at runtime, crashing the VM
with a confusing `error[E1001]: Undefined global 'print'.` fault that named the wrong
problem entirely (`print` is not undefined; it cannot be used that way). Found while
triaging PR #167's review pass (a diagnostic-quality gap surfaced, not fixed, in that
pass) and fixed here as its own concern.

**The fix.** `VisitCall` (`TypeChecker.Expressions.cs`) gains a `CheckPrintExitCall` arm
alongside the existing `input()` arm, checked first: arity (`print` exactly 1 argument,
`exit` 0 or 1), reusing **E0003** — the same code and message shape
`CheckInputCall` already uses for the other no-namespace-native builtin. A call whose
result is not the direct, statement-level expression is **E1004** — the same code
`VisitIdentifier`'s namespace-as-value arm already uses for the identical shape of
mistake, a compile-time-only construct referenced where a runtime value is expected;
no new code for either check. Position is tracked by two one-shot context flags rather
than threading a parameter through every `Visit` call: `_isStatementPositionCall` is set
only around the direct top-level expression of an `ExpressionStmt` (and, after the first
red-then-green cycle exposed the gap, also around a lambda's expression-body and a
lambda block's final implicit-return statement — both now routed through a shared
`VisitStatementPositionExpression` helper — because `xs.each(x => print(x))` is the
load-bearing existing idiom across the integration-test suite and a lambda's return
value is never surfaced to user code by a void-consuming higher-order method like
`each`, exactly like a bare statement's discarded result); `_isCallCalleePosition` is set
only around the synchronous `Visit(node.Callee)` call in `VisitCall`, so
`VisitIdentifier`'s new bare-reference rejection (mirroring the `NamespaceDecl`-as-value
arm exactly, same `E1004` code, same `Error`/`UnresolvedDecl` §3.1.1 shape) fires only
for a genuine bare reference, never for the identifier being visited as its own call's
callee. Both flags are one-shot — consumed immediately at the top of `VisitCall` — so a
nested call (`print(foo())`) never inherits the outer position. `input` is untouched:
it is a real global and was never affected by this bug class.

**Scope, deliberately narrow.** Only `print`/`exit` are touched — `input()` already has
a correct arity/type check and a genuine runtime value, proven unaffected by a direct
empirical check (`y := input` compiles and runs cleanly, unlike the identical shape for
`print`). No other builtin or user function has this "no runtime representation outside
one recognised shape" property, so the fix does not generalise past these two names.

**Empirical before/after, confirmed via the CLI.** `y := print("x")`, `print()`,
`print("a", "b")`, `y := print` — each previously crashed the VM at runtime with
`error[E1001]: Undefined global 'print'.`; each now reports a compile-time `E0003`
(arity) or `E1004` (value position) pointing at the actual mistake. The valid shapes —
`print("hello")` as a bare statement, `xs.each(x => print(x))` — are unaffected,
confirmed by the full integration-test suite (`Sprint5IncrementCTests` exercises the
`each`/`filter`-then-`each` idiom end-to-end) and a fresh CLI run.

No new opcode. No new error code — `E0003` and `E1004` both existed already; count stays
**119**.

Full detail: D-380 (the sibling correctness-batch increment this was found alongside),
the Sprint 8 Increment C `input()` arity/type check this mirrors.

### D-382 — Runtime error taxonomy corrected: `E5905`/`E5906` replace two wrong-category `E5101`/`E0004` reuses (July 2026)

Area: Runtime — error taxonomy

Supersedes: none
Superseded by: none
Refines: D-366, D-371

**The decision.** Two runtime conditions raised error codes documented as meaning
something else. Both codes involved were still `pre-release` — the last chance to fix
the taxonomy before ADR-0017 makes them immutable — so this is the correctness batch's
one deadline-bound finding.

**Finding 1 — the allocation-ceiling guard was raising `E5101`.** D-366's native-seam
hardening (`string.repeat`/`padLeft`/`padRight`, when the result would exceed the
10,000,000-character allocation ceiling) reused `E5101` ("array index out of range").
A size limit is not an index and not a bounds violation — `--explain E5101` told
someone who asked for a fifty-million-character string that their array index was out
of range.

**Finding 2 — the sort comparator was raising `E0004`.** D-371's `GrobValueComparer`
(`Grob.Vm/ArrayNatives.cs`) raised `E0004` ("argument type mismatch") when a sort key's
type does not implement `Comparable`. `E0004` is a compile-time Type-category code
(`E0001`–`E0999`); a runtime fault using a compile-time code is a category error, not
merely an imprecise label.

**Ladder outcome.** Nothing in the live registry fit either condition (Step 1 of
`allocating-an-error-code` — the E51xx bounds sub-block holds only `E5101`/`E5102`,
neither a size limit; the E59xx general-runtime sub-block's four existing codes —
`E5901` call stack overflow, `E5902` circular initialisation, `E5903` runtime failure
residual, `E5904` unhandled exception reached the top level — cover none of this).
Two codes registered in the E59xx sub-block, leaf `RuntimeError`, next free numbers
from the live tail:

- **`E5905` — "result exceeds maximum size."** Repoints the two allocation-ceiling
  throw sites in `src/Grob.Stdlib/StringMethodsPlugin.cs`: `RejectOversizedWidth`
  (guards `padLeft`/`padRight`) and `RejectOversizedRepeat` (guards `repeat`) — both
  moved from `NativeFaultException(IndexErrorLeaf, E5101, ...)` to
  `NativeFaultException(RuntimeErrorLeaf, E5905, ...)`.
- **`E5906` — "sort key type does not implement Comparable."** Repoints all three
  throw sites in `GrobValueComparer` (`src/Grob.Vm/ArrayNatives.cs`) — `Compare`'s
  kind-mismatch arm, `Compare`'s non-Comparable-kind arm and `CompareStruct`'s
  fallback for any `Struct` pairing that is not `date`/`date` or `guid`/`guid`.

`E5101` and `E0004` are **not retired** — both keep every legitimate call site.
`E5101`: `ArrayNatives.Insert`/`Remove` bounds, `VirtualMachine`'s `GetIndex`/`SetIndex`
array-receiver bounds checks and `StringMethodsPlugin`'s `Substring`/`Left`/`Right`
range checks (a real bounds violation, not an allocation ceiling — untouched). `E0004`:
all fifteen compile-time `TypeChecker` argument-type-mismatch call sites (array/map
element and key arguments, `filter`/`sort`'s `descending` argument, named-type and
primitive-member arguments, `formatAs` shape checks, `input()`'s prompt argument,
native-call argument checks, map-literal entry values, parameter defaults) — none
touched.

**A seam fix required to satisfy the sort-comparator's own acceptance test.**
`GrobValueComparer`'s three throws used `GrobRuntimeException` directly, not
`NativeFaultException` — they bypassed the native-throw seam entirely.
`ArrayNatives.Sort` unwrapped LINQ's wrapping `InvalidOperationException` and rethrew
the raw exception without ever calling `TryRaiseRuntimeGrobError`, so a Grob script
could not catch a sort-comparator fault with `try`/`catch` at all; only a C#-level
`Assert.Throws<GrobRuntimeException>` ever saw it. Repointing the code alone would not
have satisfied the requirement that "sorting by a key that is an array, a map or a
user struct" be catchable as a `GrobError` from Grob source, so the three throw sites
were also switched to `NativeFaultException`, and `Sort`'s unwrap-catch type pattern
was switched from `is GrobRuntimeException inner` to `is NativeFaultException inner`.
The fault now propagates out of `Sort`'s `Implementation` call, is caught by
`VirtualMachine.cs`'s `Call`-opcode handler, and `TryRaiseRuntimeGrobError` makes it
catchable via `try`/`catch (e: RuntimeError)`, falling back to a top-level
`GrobRuntimeException` carrying `E5906` when uncaught. This is a **behaviour
improvement** (previously-uncatchable → catchable), proven by a new
`Sort_ByUncomparableArrayKey_CaughtByTryCatch` integration test
(`Sprint9IncrementC0a1Tests.cs`) — no equivalent Grob-source fixture existed before
this entry.

**A user-visible behaviour change, recorded rather than silently absorbed.**
`Sprint9StringInstanceMethodsTests.cs`'s `Repeat_ExceedsAllocationCeiling_CaughtByTryCatch`
caught the allocation-ceiling fault as `catch (e: IndexError)`. Moving the leaf from
`IndexError` to `RuntimeError` breaks that fixture as written — a Grob script written
against the old (wrong) taxonomy that specifically catches `IndexError` around a
`repeat`/`padLeft`/`padRight` call would stop catching the fault. Updated to
`catch (e: RuntimeError)` in the same commit. `Substring_OutOfRange_CaughtByTryCatch`
and the array `insert`/`remove` bounds catch fixtures are unaffected — those stay on
the genuine `E5101`/`IndexError` path.

**A pre-existing, unrelated finding — reported, not fixed.** `E5102` ("substring
bounds out of range") is defined in `ErrorCatalog` and the registry but has no throw
site: `Substring`/`Left`/`Right` all reuse `E5101` instead. Out of scope here (not one
of the two named findings); noted for a future correctness pass rather than folded
into this one.

**Registration.** Three-location lockstep in `docs/design/grob-error-codes.md`
(summary index rows, full `### E5905`/`### E5906` entries citing this decision,
canonical total line) and the `ErrorCatalog` descriptors (`Grob.Core`) — count moves
**119 → 121**, re-verified green by the D-316 consistency gate
(`Grob.Consistency.Tests`), including its standing anchor test
(`ErrorCodeCountTests.Corpus_HasTheExpectedLiveCountOf121`, renamed and updated in the
same commit).

This closes the correctness batch's only ADR-0017-deadline item — both codes were
still `pre-release`, the last point at which the taxonomy could be corrected rather
than carried permanently.

Cites D-366 (allocation-ceiling guard, the source of the `E5101` misuse), D-371 (sort
comparator, the source of the `E0004` misuse and the array query-member surface the
comparator belongs to), D-284 (the ten-leaf `GrobError` hierarchy — `RuntimeError` is
the correct leaf for both), ADR-0017 (error-code immutability once shipped — the
reason this had a deadline), ADR-0014 (the `E5xxx` Runtime category range and
numbering scheme).

### D-383 — `for...in` snapshots contents, not just the count, for both collection types (July 2026)

Area: Language semantics / Compiler — iteration
Supersedes: none
Superseded by: none
Refines: D-379, D-378

**Why D-379 needed refining.** D-379 ratified "snapshot the bound at loop entry" and aligned
arrays to maps. The phrasing hid a distinction that turns out to be decisive: **snapshotting the
count is not the same as snapshotting the contents**, and the two collection types were doing
different things.

- `EmitMapForIn` materialises a **copy of the keys** into a synthetic local, then reads each
  value live from the live map (D-378).
- A count-only array snapshot would capture the length but index into the **live** array.

For maps the difference looked immaterial. For arrays it is not:

```grob
xs := [1, 2, 3]
for x in xs {
    xs.remove(0)
}
```

With the length captured as 3 and the array shrinking beneath it, the third iteration reads
`xs[2]` on a one-element array and faults mid-loop. The **current** live bound handles this
gracefully — the loop ends early. So D-379 as written would have made removal-during-
iteration crash where it does not today: a regression introduced by a decision intended to
improve predictability.

**The larger problem that investigation exposed.** D-378 recorded, as accepted permissive
behaviour, that a key removed mid-loop is **still visited** and its `v = m[k]` read **degrades to
`nil`**. But `for k, v in m` binds `v` as **non-nullable `V`** (D-374). A `nil` flowing into a
non-nullable binding contradicts one of Grob's foundational guarantees — *non-nullable types are
guaranteed non-nil* — and it is exactly the class of unsoundness explicit nullability exists to
prevent. A count-only array snapshot would have replicated it (an out-of-range read would need to
yield `nil` into a non-nullable `x`, or crash).

So the map path had a soundness hole, and D-379 would have propagated it to arrays.

**The decision.** `for...in` **snapshots the contents at loop entry, for both collection types.**

- **Arrays** copy the element sequence into a synthetic local before the loop and iterate the
  copy.
- **Maps** copy key-**value** pairs, not keys alone — extending `EmitMapForIn`'s existing
  materialisation rather than replacing it.

The resulting rule is statable without knowing which collection is held: **you iterate exactly
what was present when the loop started.** No crash, no silently skipped element, and no `nil`
entering a non-nullable binding. Mutation during iteration remains permitted; it has no
effect on what this loop visits.

**The copy is shallow, deliberately.** Under D-372's reference semantics the copied entries hold
the *same* `GrobArray`/`GrobMap`/`GrobStruct` references. Mutating an element's or a value's own
contents **is** visible inside the loop:

```grob
rows := [[1], [2]]
for r in rows {
    r.append(9)        // visible — same GrobArray
    rows.append([3])   // not visited — sequence frozen at entry
}
```

Only the sequence and the entry set are frozen. This follows from D-372 and is stated here so it
is not mistaken for an oversight or "fixed" into a deep copy later.

**Rejected alternatives.**

- **Count-only snapshot with a live read.** Replicates the map's unsoundness on the array path
  and must either fault out of range or force `nil` into a non-nullable binding. The truest
  mirror of the map's *current* behaviour, and rejected precisely because that behaviour is the
  defect.
- **Leave arrays live.** Graceful on removal, but keeps the two-rule inconsistency D-379 exists
  to remove.
- **Keys-only for maps.** The status quo, and the source of the soundness hole.

**Cost, and the obligation to measure it.** This adds one array copy per array loop and one
additional value copy per map loop (the keys copy already exists). For large collections that is
a real allocation cost against a previously copy-free array path. The implementing increment
**must** run the benchmark suite and report the delta against D-313's two-axis gate — 5% per
sprint, 12% cumulative — and **surface a breach rather than absorb it**. If the cost is
unacceptable on measurement, that is a finding to bring back, not a reason to weaken the
semantics quietly: D-313's standing rule is that a baseline is never updated to absorb a known
regression.

**Implementation consequence.** Both paths change shipped behaviour. The increment must enumerate
every test, fixture and validation script whose behaviour changes and report the list before
editing — a test may be updated to assert the new correct behaviour, never weakened to
accommodate it.

No new opcode. No new error code; count unchanged at **121**.

Full detail: D-379 (the decision this refines), D-378 (the map materialisation and the recorded
`nil`-degradation this closes), D-373 (the array live-bound finding), D-374 (`v` bound as
non-nullable `V`), D-372 (reference semantics, hence the shallow copy), D-313 (the benchmark
gate this must be measured against), and `grob-language-fundamentals.md`'s `for...in` section,
which should state the contents-snapshot guarantee once the increment lands.

### D-384 — `for...in` contents-snapshot lands: arrays and maps (July 2026)

Area: Compiler / VM — iteration
Supersedes: none
Superseded by: none
Refines: D-383, D-379, D-378, D-374, D-373, D-372

Lands what D-383 ratified. PR #169.

**Array mechanism.** `EmitArrayForIn` (`Compiler.ControlFlow.cs`) no longer keeps a synthetic
local holding the live array reference. Immediately after visiting the iterable expression it
emits a new internal `GetProperty` case, `"$snapshot"` (`VirtualMachine.cs`), and stores *that*
result in the synthetic local instead — `new GrobArray(array.Elements)`, a genuine shallow copy
via `GrobArray`'s existing copying constructor. The synthetic-local count is unchanged (2:
snapshot array, counter) — the live-reference local is repurposed to hold the copy instead.
`"$snapshot"` is deliberately unreachable from Grob source: the lexer's `IsIdentStart` forbids `$`
from starting an identifier, so no `MemberAccessExpr` the parser produces can ever address it —
it cannot leak into D-373's recorded array method-fallthrough gap as an accidental user-visible
feature. No new opcode: `GetProperty` already exists, and adding a dispatch case to it is the same
technique already used for maps' `keys`/`values`. Rejected: a public `arr.copy()`/`clone()` method,
which would need type-checker arity/type-argument wiring for a purely internal compiler concern —
more machinery than the one concern needed.

**Map mechanism — reuses, adds no VM code.** `EmitMapForIn` already materialised `keys` once into
a synthetic local (D-378); this lands a second, parallel materialisation of `values` (`$values`),
taken back-to-back with `$keys` before the loop starts so no mutation can occur between the two
snapshots and the two arrays stay index-aligned. This reuses the VM's **pre-existing** `"values"`
`GetProperty` case for maps (built for D-377's query-member surface, already index-aligned with
`"keys"` per D-378) — so the map side needed **zero VM changes**, only the compiler emission. Each
iteration's value read moves from a live `map[k]` (`GetIndex` against the live `GrobMap`) to
`values[i]` (`GetIndex` against the snapshot). `$map` itself stays a synthetic local for the whole
loop even though nothing reads it again after the two materialisation calls — kept for
slot-contiguity simplicity rather than adding an inner scope to release it early. Synthetic count
goes from 3 (`$map`, `$keys`, counter) to 4 (`$map`, `$keys`, `$values`, counter). Considered and
rejected: an array-of-pairs snapshot (needs a new VM/native tuple-building mechanism, no existing
precedent) and a copied `GrobMap` (needs a new clone mechanism for `GrobMap`'s backing
`OrderedDictionary`, heavier than two flat arrays). The parallel-arrays option reused what already
existed and added no new machinery — the "least new machinery" criterion the D-383 plan-mode gate
asked to weigh.

**Synthetic-local lifetime, nesting, closures, break/continue — no change needed to the shared
machine.** `EmitForInLoop`'s while-machine already treats synthetic locals as ordinary `LocalVar`
entries in `_localScopes`/`_nextSlot`, generically handling any `syntheticCount` and cleaning up
with one `EmitScopeCleanup` call at loop exit; `break`/`continue` already route through
`LocalsAboveBaseSlot(ctx.BaseSlot)`/`EmitScopeCleanup`, whose per-local `Captured` check already
emits `CloseUpvalue` rather than a blind pop for any captured slot, synthetic or iteration
variable alike. None of this needed to change — it was proven, not just reasoned about, by new
tests: same-array and array-inside-map nesting (no synthetic-local collision), break/continue over
both new lowerings (clean exit, no stack residue) and a new map closure-capture test
(`MapForInBodyCapture_PerIterationValueClosesOnBodyExit`) against the form's now-four-synthetic-
local shape. The pre-existing Sprint 5 Increment D array closure/break-capture tests
(`ForInBodyCapture_PerIterationItemClosesOnBodyExit`, `BreakWithCapture_ClosesCapturedLocalOnEarlyExit`)
continued to pass unmodified against the new array lowering.

**The soundness hole is closed.** `v` can no longer be `nil` in `for k, v in m`'s non-nullable `V`
binding (D-378's recorded degradation, D-374's binding). `MapSoundness_RemovingAndClearingDuringIteration_ValueNeverDegradesToNil`
proves it across both `m.remove(k)` and `m.clear()` in the same iteration body — every iteration's
`v` is read from the entry-time values snapshot, unaffected by any live mutation. The pre-existing
Sprint 9 Increment C0b-2b test that had recorded the old `nil`-degrade as accepted, permissive
behaviour was itself updated to assert the corrected behaviour end to end.

**Shallow-copy semantics, proven by test.** `ShallowCopy_MutatingElementContentsVisible_AppendingOuterArrayNotVisited`:
`rows := [[1], [2]]; for r in rows { r.append(9); rows.append([3]) }` — `r.append(9)` mutates the
*same* underlying `GrobArray` reference `rows` holds (visible: both `rows[0][1]` and `rows[1][1]`
read `9` afterwards), while `rows.append([3])` inside the body is never visited by the loop itself
(it still runs exactly the entry-time count, 2 iterations) even though it grows the live `rows` to
4 elements by the time the loop finishes.

**Full breaking-change list.**

- `tests/Grob.Integration.Tests/Sprint9IncrementC0b2bTests.cs`:
  `ForIn_RemovingCurrentMapDuringIteration_KeepsFixedIterationCount_ValueReadsNilForRemovedKey`
  renamed to `..._ValueReadsEntryTimeValue`; expected stdout changed from `"1\nnil\n2\n"` to
  `"1\n2\n2\n"`; the doc comment recording the `nil`-degrade as accepted behaviour rewritten to
  describe the corrected guarantee.
- `tests/Grob.Compiler.Tests/CompilerForInTests.cs`: `Map_MaterialisesKeysOnceBeforeTheLoop`
  renamed `Map_MaterialisesKeysAndValuesOnceBeforeTheLoop`, its exact `GetProperty` count
  assertion changed 2 → 3 (keys, values, length); `Map_ReadsKeyThenValueByIndex` renamed
  `Map_ReadsKeyThenValueByIndex_BothFromTheSnapshotArrays`, same `GetIndex` count (2) but now
  asserted against the snapshot-array operand source rather than the live map; new test
  `ArraySingle_MaterialisesSnapshotOnceBeforeTheLoop` added for the array form's new shape.
  During PR review CodeRabbit correctly found both new/changed materialisation-offset assertions
  anchored against `OpCode.Loop`'s own offset — vacuously true, since `Loop` is emitted after the
  entire condition and body, so any in-loop instruction satisfies "before the loop". Fixed in the
  same PR before merge with a `LoopTop` helper decoding the actual backward-jump target, plus
  explicit `PropertyName` assertions on the `GetProperty` constant operands.
- New file `tests/Grob.Integration.Tests/ForInContentsSnapshotTests.cs` (11 tests): array
  append/removal during iteration, the map soundness case, a mid-loop map value update, the
  shallow-copy case above, same-array and array-inside-map nesting, break/continue over both new
  lowerings, the map closure-capture case and an explicit numeric-range-unaffected regression.
- No gold-master/error-example fixture pair and no validation/smoke-gate `.grob` script mutates a
  collection inside its own `for...in` body — confirmed by a full-repo search; nothing else
  required updating. The pre-existing array bytecode-shape tests (`ArraySingle_UsesLessIntAndArrayOps`,
  `ArrayIndex_UsesLessIntAndArrayOps`) assert opcode presence rather than exact counts and needed
  no change; confirmed still green against the new `$snapshot` emission.

**Numeric range confirmed untouched.** `EmitRangeForIn` received no code change. A new explicit
regression test (`NumericRangeForIn_UnaffectedByTheSnapshotChange`) and the pre-existing Sprint 4
Increment C range tests all continued to pass unmodified.

**Benchmark delta, measured against D-313's gate — the hard obligation D-383 set.** Two new VM
benchmarks (`Run_ArrayForIn`, `Run_MapForIn`, `bench/Grob.Benchmarks/Vm/VmBenchmarks.cs`) plus
fixtures (a 1,000-element array, a 1,000-entry map) land with this increment. Neither benchmark
existed before this change, so there was no prior committed baseline for a CI run to compare
against; the delta was instead measured directly and locally — the same fixtures run once against
the pre-fix compiler/VM code (isolated via `git stash` of only the two production files) and once
against the fix, back to back on the same machine (`dotnet run --configuration Release --project
bench/Grob.Benchmarks -- --filter '*ForIn*'`):

- Array `for...in` (1,000 elements): Mean 534.2 µs → 554.5 µs (**+3.8%**); Allocated 546.31 KB →
  570.61 KB (**+4.4%**).
- Map `for...in` (1,000 entries): Mean 859.6 µs → 803.5 µs (**−6.5%**, faster — within measurement
  noise, not a real improvement); Allocated 1015.74 KB → 1062.89 KB (**+4.6%**).

Both comfortably under D-313's 5%-per-sprint / 12%-cumulative thresholds and D-333's 10%
allocation axis — no breach to surface. This was a **local, ad hoc measurement**, not a run
through the canonical `benchmark.yml` CI workflow, and no committed baseline JSON was hand-edited
(D-313's ratchet-trap rule) — the two new benchmarks' first *committed* baseline is established by
the next `benchmark.yml` run, as for any newly introduced benchmark. Recorded precisely because it
matters to the obligation: at the time of this change the `vm` benchmark category is
`"gating": false` in `bench/Grob.Benchmarks/baseline/policy.json`, so this obligation was
discharged by direct measurement and this log entry, not by an automatic CI gate.

No new opcode. No new error code; count confirmed unchanged at **121** against the live registry
at landing time.

Full detail: D-383 (the decision this lands), D-379 (the bound-only snapshot it refines), D-378
(the map's keys-only materialisation and the recorded `nil`-degradation this closes), D-374 (`v`'s
non-nullable binding, the guarantee at stake), D-373 (the array live-bound finding), D-372
(reference semantics, hence the shallow copy), D-313 (the benchmark gate measured against), and
`grob-language-fundamentals.md`'s `for...in` section (updated alongside D-383 to state the
contents-snapshot guarantee and the shallow-copy consequence).
