### D-385 — Benchmark harness correctness: category semantics, LOH tripwire, CPU-heterogeneity gap, composition-root fidelity, fixture design and the gating matrix (July 2026)

Area: Tooling — benchmarking
Supersedes: none
Superseded by: none
Refines: D-313, D-333, D-302, D-309

**Type: decision-only session. No source changes, no harness changes were made under this entry —
phase 3 applies what is decided here.** Runs against the corpus carrying D-356 through D-384, plus
`docs/design/bench-allocation-attribution.md` (phase 1's findings note, committed on
`bench/allocation-attribution` alongside this entry). Every empirical figure below is phase 1's,
cited rather than restated from memory.

**Context — why this decision exists.** The `Benchmarks` CI run on `0125bae` failed for a reason
unrelated to the change under test. Investigation, deepened by phase 1's differential-fixture
measurement, found six things wrong with what the gate measures or reports, not with the change it
was run against.

**Q1 — category semantics.** `VmBenchmarks.RunSource` (`bench/Grob.Benchmarks/Vm/VmBenchmarks.cs`)
runs the entire pipeline — `Lexer.Scan → Parser.Parse → TypeChecker.Check → Compiler.Compile →
vm.Run` — inside the `vm` category's measured region, so a compiler regression and a VM regression
are currently indistinguishable in the same number. This is not an open design question:
`grob-benchmarking-strategy.md` §4.2 already specifies the VM category uses "hand-constructed
`Chunk` instances — the compiler is not involved"; the implementation drifted from a standing
decision. Meanwhile §4.3's `endToEnd` category — the thirteen/eleven validation-suite scripts
through the real pipeline, the *primary* gate per D-313/§9 — has never been implemented; no
`Grob.Benchmarks.EndToEnd` namespace exists, and `policy.json`'s `endToEnd` category has always
had zero fresh benchmarks to compare (F8). **Decided:** the current nine full-pipeline benchmarks
(`Run_DeclAndArith` … `Run_MapForIn`, plus phase 1's `attr-*` fixtures) are renamed into a new
`endToEnd` category — real pipeline-to-execution content against F8, not a cosmetic label, though
narrower than §4.3's full validation-suite corpus. `vm` is rebuilt to hoist compilation into
`[GlobalSetup]`/a pre-built `Chunk` so the benchmark method measures `vm.Run(chunk)` alone,
restoring §4.2's already-documented intent — phase 3 must confirm a pre-built `Chunk` reused
across BDN iterations does not carry state between runs that would invalidate the isolation (a
fresh `VirtualMachine` per invocation, as today, is assumed to remain necessary). **Rejected:**
maintaining both under the existing names with no semantic change (the size of the problem phase 1
quantified — 86.4% of `Run_ArrayForIn`'s allocation is fixture setup — demands more than a label);
building the full §4.3 validation-suite corpus inside this same decision's implementation (out of
proportion to a "make categories honest" fix; staged below). **Cost:** the renamed `endToEnd`
category does not yet match §4.3's description in full (it is nine representative scripts, not the
validation suite), so F8 is *narrowed*, not closed, by this entry alone.

**Q2 — the LOH tripwire.** `policy.json`'s `lohTripwireBytes` (85,000 B) is the .NET Large Object
Heap's actual single-object promotion threshold, but `BenchCheck.BreachesLohTripwire`
(`tooling/Grob.BenchCheck/BenchCheck.cs`) checks it against `Memory.BytesAllocatedPerOperation` —
BenchmarkDotNet's summary output carries no per-object size data, so the check cannot and never
could detect a large-object promotion; it is, and per D-333's own text was always documented as,
"any benchmark, gating or not, whose fresh allocation meets or exceeds this fails outright" — a
total-per-operation ceiling. The gap phase 1 quantified is not the mechanism's identity but its
one-size-fits-all threshold: both `for...in` benchmarks, after D-383's contents-snapshot, sit
574.54 KB / 1066.81 KB per operation — 6.9×/12.9× over 85,000 B — a shape the LOH byte count was
never chosen to fit. **Decided:** keep the mechanism exactly as it functions today; redocument its
name and rationale in `grob-benchmarking-strategy.md` §9 and this log as a **total-allocation
ceiling**, explicitly not an LOH detector; phase 3 derives a per-category (or per-fixture-shape)
threshold from phase 1's measured values — the pipeline floor (≈44 KB), per-native-call cost
(≈186 B/call) and the two `for...in` figures above are the starting data — rather than one constant
borrowed from an unrelated CLR concept. **Rejected:** implementing genuine large-object detection
(would need a different diagnostic than `[MemoryDiagnoser]`'s summary output provides, a
disproportionate cost for the signal gained); removing the tripwire outright (it is the only
mechanical catch for a D-332-class defect — an informational category silently landing on
oversized allocation — and phase 1 changed nothing about that need). **Cost:** phase 3 owns
choosing and justifying the new threshold(s); until it lands, the tripwire keeps firing on the
`for...in` benchmarks' legitimate allocation, which is why the CI run at `0125bae` failed on a
change unrelated to it.

**Q3 — the time axis under CPU heterogeneity.** The CI run reported "CPU mismatch — fresh 'AMD
EPYC 7763' vs rolling baseline 'Intel Xeon Platinum 8370C'" for the `vm` category, and phase 1
confirms `vm.json`/`vm.origin.json` are both captured on the Xeon while the fresh run landed on the
EPYC — D-333's `SameCpu` guard working exactly as designed, degrading the time comparison to
informational while allocation still gates. Separately, `compile.origin.json`'s
`HostEnvironmentInfo.ProcessorName` reads `"Unknown processor"` (a pre-D-333, BenchmarkDotNet
0.14.0 capture) — `BenchCheck.IsUnknownProcessor` never treats this as a match to anything, so the
`compile` category's cumulative axis is permanently informational until someone deliberately
re-captures that file. **This is not a fresh finding — D-333 already logged it explicitly**
("a known, logged gap (D-333), not a silent one") and deliberately declined to re-freeze it in the
same session. What D-313 itself does not yet say, read on its own, is that this gap exists at all;
a reader of D-313 alone is told a 12%-cumulative guarantee the compile category currently cannot
deliver. **Decided:** record an amendment to D-313 in this entry (`Refines: D-313`; D-313's own
entry is never edited) stating plainly that the compile category's cumulative time axis is inert
on GitHub-hosted runners pending a deliberate `compile.origin.json` re-capture — closing the gap this session cites ADR-0018's "documented gate = enforced gate"
precedent for, without re-opening D-333's own, already-correct, CPU-identity mechanism. **Rejected:**
pinning a self-hosted or dedicated-hardware runner (disproportionate — D-333's per-baseline CPU
check already handles heterogeneity correctly; the problem is a documentation gap, not a mechanism
gap); a CPU-independent between-benchmark ratio signal (a genuinely different, more invasive
measurement technique with no demonstrated need here — out of scope for this entry). **Cost:**
none beyond documentation — no code or baseline changes follow from this Q; `compile.origin.json`
remains un-recaptured, by design, until a future deliberate act.

**Q4 — benchmark fidelity: which composition root.** `VmBenchmarks.RunSource` constructs a bare
`VirtualMachine` and, as of phase 1's branch, registers `new StringMethodsPlugin()` uniformly
across every fixture (including the five pre-existing ones), rather than mirroring the CLI's
`Grob.Cli.PluginRegistration.RegisterAll` (twelve plugins, four needing `IRandomSource`/
`IEnvironment`/`IStandardStreams`/`IClock` injection). **Decided:** ratify phase 1's stopgap as the
permanent approach — `StringMethodsPlugin` is pure (no capability injection) and its one-time
registration cost cancels out of every pairwise fixture subtraction; mirroring the full composition
root would require capability-interface fakes purely to satisfy registration, for natives no
current VM-dispatch benchmark calls. Document, per phase 1 §4's finding, that array/map
instance-method dispatch (`ArrayNatives.GetMethod`, a fresh `NativeFunction`/closure/display-class
triple built on every call) is a structurally distinct and more expensive native-call path than the
Stdlib-plugin path `StringMethodsPlugin` represents (cached delegate, looked up once via
`GetGlobal`) — "bytes per native call" is not one number across Grob's ~99 natives, and any future
benchmark or optimisation argument citing a native-call cost must say which path it means.
**Rejected:** mirroring `RegisterAll` in full (harness complexity for capability interfaces no
benchmark under this category exercises; a future increment that specifically wants to measure a
capability-backed native — `date`, `fs`, `process` — can register that one plugin directly without
adopting the whole composition root). **Cost:** none — this ratifies work already done on
`bench/allocation-attribution` rather than commissioning new work.

**Q5 — fixture design.** Whole-script benchmarks cannot build a fixture outside their own measured
region, so perfect isolation is unattainable; phase 1's differential-fixture technique (subtracting
successive fixtures differing by exactly one thing) is the working answer, not a compromise to
improve on. **Decided:** every whole-script benchmark is documented as measuring the whole script,
compilation included, unless and until Q1's `vm` rebuild lands; phase 1's `attr-empty`,
`attr-range`, `attr-native` and `attr-build` fixtures — despite their doc comments today marking
them "phase 1 allocation-attribution fixture (throwaway)" — become permanent companion fixtures
under whichever category ends up hosting them post-Q1 (most naturally `endToEnd`, since they are
full-pipeline runs); the two fixtures phase 1 named as missing are added: `attr-map-build` (map
construction with no second loop, isolating the interpolation-vs-second-snapshot split
§6 left unresolved for `Run_MapForIn`'s 504,084 B delta) and an empty-body snapshot fixture
(isolating the unexplained ≈55 KB gap in phase 1 §5's ≈3.3×-over-prediction finding for
`array-for-in`'s snapshot-plus-iteration cost). **Rejected:** discarding the `attr-*` fixtures as
genuinely throwaway now that the harness redesign consumes their data directly — their doc comments
are updated in phase 3 to drop "throwaway" once they are wired into the permanent suite.
**Cost:** two new fixture files plus their benchmark methods; no fixture reduces existing coverage.

**Q6 — what gates, what is informational.** `policy.json` today: `compile` gates (both time axes
plus allocation), `vm`/`endToEnd` gate on allocation only (time informational). This already
matches D-313/§9's documented build-out stand-in — "until end-to-end becomes live... compile-time
gates cumulatively... VM execution stays informational" — it is not a bug, contrary to the initial
framing that prompted this session. **Decided:** state the matrix explicitly in this entry (a second
amendment recorded against D-313, not an edit to it) so it is asserted once rather than
reconstructed by a reader from `policy.json` plus two
separate decisions: **`compile`** gates on per-sprint time (significance-aware, D-333), cumulative
time (until `compile.origin.json` is re-captured — Q3) and allocation (percent + LOH-ceiling, Q2);
**`vm`/`endToEnd`** gate on allocation only, time informational, as the documented build-out stand-in.
The flip condition already implied by §9 is stated explicitly: when `endToEnd` carries the full
validation-suite corpus (Q1's follow-on), it becomes the gate and `compile`/`vm` drop to
informational — a deliberate `policy.json` edit, never automatic. `stability` is confirmed as
correctly outside this matrix entirely — `StabilityRunner`'s own `tolerancePercent`/
`lastPassingHeapBytes` mechanism, never a `[Benchmark]` class `BenchCheck` compares, by design, not
oversight. **Rejected:** flipping any `gating` flag in this entry (no baseline or threshold changes
follow from a decision session; that is phase 3's, or later, deliberate act). **Cost:** none — this
Q asserts the existing, already-correct matrix in the durable record rather than changing it.

**F8 status.** Partially resolved: Q1's rename gives `endToEnd` real, if narrower-than-specified,
content, ending the "zero fresh benchmarks matched" state the CI note recorded. Not closed: the
full §4.3 validation-suite corpus is unbuilt. Proposed as a separate, later increment (see staging,
below) rather than folded into phase 3, given its size relative to the rest of this decision.

**Constraints honoured.** No baseline file is touched and no threshold is loosened by this entry —
D-313's ratchet-trap rule holds throughout; every Q either corrects what a category is named or
measures, or documents an existing, already-correct mechanism more honestly. The compile-benchmark
cumulative drift phase 1's context flagged (`Compile_TwoExpressions` +65.2%, `Compile_TenPrints`
+37.9% against origin, both suppressed as CPU mismatch) is not silently rebaselined by this entry —
it remains unmeasurable until `compile.origin.json` is deliberately re-captured (Q3), at which point
it must be measured and reported, not assumed benign.

**Staging — more than one increment.** This decision needs at least two: **phase 3** applies Q1–Q6
mechanically (the `vm`/`endToEnd` rename and rebuild, the two new `attr-*` fixtures, the
`policy.json`/strategy-doc redocumentation, the D-313/D-333 corpus amendments this entry makes) —
scoped, small, no new benchmark corpus. A **later, separate increment** builds the full §4.3
validation-suite `endToEnd` corpus that fully closes F8 and lets `endToEnd` become the actual
primary gate — larger, gated on which of the eleven/thirteen validation scripts Sprint 9 has made
runnable, and not assumed complete by this entry.

Refines D-313 (Q3's explicit compile-cumulative-inert statement; Q6's explicit gating matrix) and
D-333 (Q2's tripwire redocumentation as a total-allocation ceiling, not an LOH detector) — cites
ADR-0018 for the "documented gate = enforced gate" precedent this session applies to both. Cites
D-302, D-309 (the harness and baseline-production decisions D-313 itself refines), D-383 (the
contents-snapshot change whose allocation growth is what pushed the `for...in` benchmarks over the
LOH tripwire in the first place), and `docs/design/bench-allocation-attribution.md` for every
empirical figure above.

### D-386 — `vm` rebuilt in place, `endToEnd` left empty, attribution fixtures get their own category (July 2026)

Area: Benchmarking — categories and fixtures
Supersedes: none
Superseded by: none
Refines: D-385

D-385 settled six questions about the benchmark harness. Four of them — Q2 (per-category
allocation ceilings), Q3 (refine D-313 from this entry rather than chase a stable runner), Q4 (minimal
composition root, `StringMethodsPlugin` stopgap ratified) and Q6 (explicit gating matrix with a
stated flip condition) — stand exactly as ratified and are not touched here. This entry refines
the other two, both of which D-385's own author flagged as judgment calls rather than clean
single answers.

---

**Q1' — `vm` is rebuilt in place; `endToEnd` stays empty and F8 stays open.**

D-385 proposed moving the nine current full-pipeline fixtures (`Run_DeclAndArith` through
`Run_MapForIn`) into the `endToEnd` category, giving F8's never-captured baseline its first real
content, while `vm` was rebuilt to measure execution alone.

The rebuild half is right and is kept. The rename half is rejected, for three reasons:

1. **It contradicts `endToEnd`'s own specification.** `grob-benchmarking-strategy.md` §4.3
   defines the category as the validation-suite scripts run through the real CLI pipeline.
   `Run_DeclAndArith` and its siblings are synthetic micro-scripts. Filling a category with
   content that does not match its documented definition is precisely the documented-versus-built
   divergence this consolidation phase exists to remove — the same failure mode as the `string`
   methods, the numeric surface, `map` literal construction and the `map<K, V>` typing note.
2. **It obscures F8.** F8 names the validation-suite end-to-end baseline specifically. Recording
   it as "partially resolved" when the artefact it names still does not exist makes the remaining
   gap harder for a cold reader to see, not easier — and F8 has already survived several sprints
   partly by being easy to overlook.
3. **It is largely redundant.** Once `vm` measures execution per §4.2 and `compile` measures
   compilation, a third category measuring approximately their sum on synthetic scripts adds
   baseline surface, maintenance and noise for little additional signal.

**Ratified:** `vm` is rebuilt **in place**. The same fixtures stay in the same category;
compilation moves into `[GlobalSetup]` (or an equivalent pre-built `Chunk`) so the measured region
is `vm.Run(chunk)` alone. This restores §4.2's standing intent — *"hand-constructed `Chunk`
instances — the compiler is not involved"* — from which `VmBenchmarks.RunSource` had drifted. The
drift, not the design, was the defect.

`endToEnd` **stays empty**, and **F8 is recorded as open, not partially resolved**. It is built
properly in its own increment, against the real validation-suite corpus — materially more feasible
now that Sprint 9's consolidation has made most of those scripts runnable.

---

**Q5' — the attribution fixtures get a dedicated non-gating category.**

D-385 ratified making phase 1's `attr-*` differential fixtures permanent, hosted "under `vm`
(post-Q1 rebuild) or `endToEnd` (pre-rebuild, whichever category ends up hosting them)". Permanent
is right — the differential-fixture technique is the answer to the isolation problem, not a
workaround for it. The hosting is refined.

The `attr-*` fixtures are **instruments, not guards**. They measure the pipeline floor, loop
machinery and per-native-call overhead — diagnostic quantities, not features. Gating on them would
gate on the wrong things, and a regression in `attr-empty` means "the compiler pipeline allocates
more", which is already `compile`'s job to catch.

They are also **whole-script by nature**, which is what made D-385 want a whole-script category to
put them in. With Q1' leaving `endToEnd` empty, that home has to be something else.

**Ratified:** a dedicated **`attribution` category, `gating: false`**, hosting the `attr-*`
fixtures. The name states what they are; it gates nothing; and it leaves `endToEnd` free for its
actual specified meaning. The two fixtures phase 1 identified as missing join them:
`attr-map-build` (to split `Run_MapForIn`'s 1,000 `"k${i}"` interpolations from its second
snapshot array) and an **empty-body snapshot fixture** (to isolate the unexplained ~55 KB in phase
1 §5, where snapshot-plus-iteration measured ≈3.3× the predicted ~24 KB).

On that ~55 KB: a candidate explanation worth testing when the empty-body fixture lands is that
`GrobArray`'s only constructor takes `IEnumerable<GrobValue>` and copies via `[.. elements]`, with
no statically-known count — so the snapshot copy may grow by doubling (≈2,044 discarded slots,
≈49 KB) on the way to the final 1,000-element array (≈24 KB). That predicts ≈73–80 KB against
80,015 B measured. **Untested inference, recorded as a hypothesis for measurement, not a finding.**

---

No new opcode. No new error code; count unchanged at **121**.

Full detail: D-385 (the decision this refines, four of whose six answers stand unchanged),
`grob-benchmarking-strategy.md` §4.2 and §4.3, `docs/design/bench-allocation-attribution.md`
(phase 1's measured evidence), D-313 and D-333 (the gate this governs), and F8 in
`grob-principal-review-sprint9b.md`.

### D-387 — Benchmark harness restructure landed: vm rebuilt, attribution category, gating matrix stated explicitly (July 2026)

Area: Tooling — benchmarking (implementation)
Supersedes: none
Superseded by: none
Refines: D-385, D-386

**Phase 3a.** Applies D-385/D-386's ratified decisions to `bench/Grob.Benchmarks`,
`tooling/Grob.BenchCheck.Tests` and `grob-benchmarking-strategy.md`, then captures and reports
fresh numbers for the changed measurements. No `src/` change.

**`vm` rebuilt in place (Q1').** `VmBenchmarks.RunSource`'s full-pipeline measurement is gone.
`[GlobalSetup]` now compiles each of the five fixtures (`decl-and-arith`, `interpolation`,
`control-flow`, `array-for-in`, `map-for-in`) to a `Chunk` field once, via the same
`Lexer.Scan → Parser.Parse → TypeChecker.Check → Compiler.Compile` pipeline as before, just
moved out of the measured region. `[IterationSetup]` constructs a fresh `VirtualMachine` before
every iteration — the mechanism D-385's own text assumed would remain necessary, needed here
because `array-for-in`/`map-for-in` mutate global state (`xs`/`m`) through the same reused
`Chunk`, and a VM shared across iterations would compound that growth run over run. Each
`[Benchmark]` method is now exactly `vm.Run(chunk)`, restoring `grob-benchmarking-strategy.md`
§4.2's always-standing definition. Neither `Grob.Stdlib` nor `StringMethodsPlugin` is needed in
`VmBenchmarks` any more — none of the five fixtures call a stdlib-registered native (`xs.append`/
`m.set` are `ArrayNatives`/`MapNatives`-internal, bound directly by `GetProperty`); that
registration moved with the fixtures that actually need it.

**`endToEnd` untouched; F8 stays open (Q1').** Not populated, not renamed into. `policy.json`'s
`endToEnd` category is left exactly as it already was — declared, `gating: false`, no committed
baseline. Building it against the real validation-suite corpus is its own, later increment.

**`attribution` category created, `gating: false` (Q5').** New
`Grob.Benchmarks.Attribution.AttributionBenchmarks` (namespace `Grob.Benchmarks.Attribution`),
carrying the moved `Run_Attr*` methods and the whole-pipeline `RunSource` helper the `vm`
category used to share — the `attr-*` fixtures stay whole-script by design, since they are
differential instruments, not features to gate on. Fixtures moved from `Fixtures/Vm/` to a new
`Fixtures/Attribution/` directory; every doc comment drops "(phase 1, throwaway)" since D-385/
D-386 made them permanent. Three fixtures added. Two are the ones phase 1/D-386 named as missing:
`attr-map-build.grob` (map construction only, no second loop) and `attr-snapshot-empty.grob`
(the `attr-build` build loop plus an empty-body `for...in` over the built array, isolating the
pure contents-snapshot copy). The third, `attr-array-dispatch.grob` (`xs.contains(i)` × 1,000, no
growth), is the growth-free control for `attr-build` that phase 1 §4 recorded as missing — added
in PR #171 review, with the subtraction-hygiene rules it enforces set out under the measurements
below. Two fixtures also lost an unmatched terminal operation in that review (`print(0)` from
`attr-empty`, `print(m.length)` from `attr-map-build`): a fixture that ends with output its
counterpart lacks makes every subtraction against it include or omit that output work, so
`attr-empty` — the category's `Baseline = true` fixture, subtracted against by all six others — is
now deliberately statement-free. `policy.json` gains
`{ "name": "attribution", "namespacePrefix": "Grob.Benchmarks.Attribution", "baseline": "attribution.json", "gating": false }`.
Two new `BenchCheckTests` cases prove the mechanism (already policy-data-driven, no
`BenchCheck.cs` change needed): a deliberately large time+alloc delta in an `"attribution"`
category classifies `Informational`/`Informational`, never a regression; and the two new
fixtures classify `NewBenchmark`/`NewBenchmark` against a rolling baseline that only knows the
four pre-existing ones — the same already-correct path phase 2 flagged as "correctly working, do
not fix".

**Composition root ratified in code (D-385 Q4).** `AttributionBenchmarks.RunSource` keeps
`StringMethodsPlugin` registered uniformly across every fixture in the category, with an
in-code comment recording why: it is pure (no capability injection), and its one-time
registration cost cancels out of every pairwise subtraction. The comment also records phase 1
§4's structural finding — `ArrayNatives`/`MapNatives` instance-method dispatch (`xs.append`/
`m.set`) is reachable without any plugin registration at all, and builds a fresh
`NativeFunction`/closure/display-class triple on every call, a structurally distinct and more
expensive path than the cached, once-built `StringMethodsPlugin` natives.

**Corpus amendments (never editing D-313's or D-333's entries in place — cited, not rewritten).**
`grob-benchmarking-strategy.md`: new §4.2a documents the `attribution` category in full; §4.2
gains an implementation note recording the vm-rebuild correction; §3 and §7.1's directory trees
gain `Attribution/`; §8's baseline-file lists gain `attribution.json`/`attribution.origin.json`
(declared in `policy.json`, not yet committed — the same status `endToEnd.json`/
`endToEnd.origin.json` already have) plus a note that the committed `vm.json`/`vm.origin.json`
now describe a stale, pre-rebuild measurement pending deliberate re-capture; new §9.1 states the
gating matrix explicitly (category × time-per-sprint × time-cumulative × allocation × LOH
tripwire, all four categories) and the flip condition, and states plainly that `compile`'s
cumulative axis is inert while `compile.origin.json` carries `"Unknown processor"` — closing the
ADR-0018-style "documented gate = enforced gate" gap D-385 Q3 opened. Footer citation extended.

**The baseline distinction, stated explicitly.** Establishing a baseline for a changed
measurement is legitimate; loosening a baseline to absorb a known regression is the ratchet trap
D-313 forbids. This entry does the former only. Every number below is a **new-measurement
baseline** for `vm` (which now measures something different than its committed `vm.json`/
`vm.origin.json` ever did) and a **first measurement** for `attribution` (which has never had a
committed baseline) — none is a revised threshold, and `compile`'s baselines are untouched.

**Fresh numbers — local machine, not a canonical baseline.** Measured via
`dotnet run -c Release --project bench/Grob.Benchmarks -- --filter '*VmBenchmarks*' '*AttributionBenchmarks*'`
on the same machine phase 1 used (Intel Core i5-8400 CPU @ 2.80GHz, Coffee Lake, Windows 11
10.0.26200.8875, .NET 10.0.10, BenchmarkDotNet 0.15.8) — **not** the canonical `windows-latest`
`benchmark.yml` capture `grob-benchmarking-strategy.md` §8.1/§8.2 requires for a committed
baseline. Per §8.2, local results are never committed as baselines; the maintainer pushing this
branch and dispatching `benchmark.yml` is a deliberate follow-up action, out of scope here.

`vm` (execution only, `vm.Run(chunk)`):

| Benchmark | Mean | Allocated |
|---|---:|---:|
| `Run_DeclAndArith` | 28.97 μs | 2,344 B |
| `Run_Interpolation` | 34.49 μs | 3,880 B |
| `Run_ControlFlow` | 207.94 μs | 2,504 B |
| `Run_ArrayForIn` | 1,244.41 μs | 531,616 B |
| `Run_MapForIn` | 1,970.83 μs | 1,033,320 B |

`attribution` (whole pipeline, `StringMethodsPlugin` registered):

| Benchmark | Mean | Allocated |
|---|---:|---:|
| `Run_AttrEmpty` | 6.58 μs | 44,172 B |
| `Run_AttrRange` | 75.34 μs | 46,149 B |
| `Run_AttrNative` | 210.05 μs | 232,032 B |
| `Run_AttrBuild` | 280.05 μs | 508,316 B |
| `Run_AttrMapBuild` (new) | 483.34 μs | 941,592 B |
| `Run_AttrSnapshotEmpty` (new) | 457.04 μs | 583,732 B |

Derived, reproducing phase 1's figures almost exactly on the same machine: loop machinery
(`attr-range` − `attr-empty`) = 1,977 B; Stdlib-plugin per-native-call overhead
((`attr-native` − `attr-range`) ÷ 1000) ≈ 186 B/call; **combined array-member-dispatch tax plus
growth** (`attr-build` − `attr-native`) = 276,284 B over 1,000 `append` calls.

**That last figure is a combined cost, not array growth alone** — a correction to how the same
subtraction was first labelled in this entry, caught in PR #171 review. Phase 1 §4 established
that `attr-build` and `attr-native` sit on structurally different native paths: `"x".upper()` is a
Stdlib-plugin native registered once and reached by `GetGlobal`, whereas `xs.append(i)` is bound
fresh by `OpCode.GetProperty` on every call, allocating a `NativeFunction`/delegate/display-class
triple each time. Differencing across that boundary therefore carries the dispatch tax as well as
the growth, exactly as phase 1 warned ("not 'per-native-call overhead plus growth'… stated as
inference, not measured directly"), and phase 1 recorded the absence of a dedicated fixture to
separate them. **This entry closes that gap:** a seventh fixture, `attr-array-dispatch.grob`
(`xs.contains(i)` × 1,000 on an array that never grows), is the growth-free control. `contains`
and `append` are both arity-1 `ArrayNatives` bound by the same `GetProperty` path and capturing
the receiver identically, so they pay the same per-call triple and `attr-build` −
`attr-array-dispatch` isolates growth alone. **Its number is not yet measured** — no local
re-run was taken for it, and only the `benchmark.yml` workflow produces a committable baseline —
so the isolated array-growth figure lands with the canonical `attribution.json` capture, which is
already a follow-up below.

**New — the snapshot hypothesis, measured, no action taken.** Pure contents-snapshot cost
(`attr-snapshot-empty` − `attr-build`) = **75,416 B**, inside D-386's ≈73–80 KB doubling-hypothesis
prediction for `GrobArray`'s `IEnumerable<GrobValue>`-constructor copy. Subtracting this from
phase 1's recorded `array-for-in − attr-build` figure (80,015 B) leaves ≈4,599 B (≈4.6 B/iteration)
attributable to the iteration body itself (1,000 unboxed int accumulations) — small and plausible.
This is consistent with, not proof of, the doubling explanation. **Reported; no action taken.**
Any fix is a separate, measured decision.

**New — the map-build split.** `attr-map-build` isolates the build loop alone (941,592 B). The
rebuilt `vm` category's `Run_MapForIn` no longer shares a measurement basis with it (one excludes
compilation, the other is whole-pipeline), so the split uses phase 1's frozen full-pipeline
`Run_MapForIn` figure (1,092,413 B,
`docs/design/bench-allocation-attribution.md`) as the comparison basis instead: second-loop-plus-
values-snapshot ≈ 1,092,413 − 941,592 = **150,821 B**; the map-build loop itself (1,000
interpolations, `map.set` calls and map growth) ≈ 941,592 − 44,172 = **897,420 B** over the
pipeline floor.

**Phase 3b is not addressed here.** Per-category allocation ceilings (D-385 Q2) need this
increment's numbers first; the existing LOH tripwire is left exactly as it fires today.

No new opcode. No new error code; count unchanged at **121**.

### D-388 — `GrobArray`'s doubling-copy hypothesis refuted by direct measurement; no fix needed (July 2026)

Area: Core — `GrobArray` construction
Supersedes: none
Superseded by: none
Refines: D-386 (closes the snapshot-copy doubling hypothesis it recorded but did not test)

**The hypothesis under test.** D-386/D-387 recorded that `GrobArray`'s constructor
(`_elements = elements is null ? [] : [.. elements]`) might grow its copy by doubling because the
parameter's *static* type is `IEnumerable<GrobValue>`, not `ICollection<GrobValue>` — predicting
≈73–80 KB of discarded slots for a 1,000-element copy against a ≈24,576 B ideal, a figure D-387's
`attr-snapshot-empty` − `attr-build` differential (75,416 B) landed inside. D-313 requires
measurement before any optimisation; this increment was that measurement, planned as: apply an
explicit `ICollection<GrobValue>` fast-path branch, remeasure and report confirmation or
refutation rather than defending the branch regardless of the result.

**Refuted.** The hypothesis is wrong. Applying the fast-path fix
(`elements switch { null => [], ICollection<GrobValue> c => new List<GrobValue>(c), _ => [.. elements] }`)
produced **byte-identical** allocation to the unmodified constructor under *both* measurements —
but they are two different scopes and carry two different figures, which must not be conflated:

- **Isolated constructor copy** — `GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread` around the exact call
  shape `VirtualMachine.cs`'s `$snapshot` property uses (`new GrobArray(existingArray.Elements)`,
  `Elements`' runtime type always `List<GrobValue>`), 1,000-element source: **24,080 B** before and
  24,080 B after — already inside the ≈24,576 B ideal, so there is no doubling to remove.
- **Whole-pipeline differential** — `attr-snapshot-empty` − `attr-build`: **74,560 B** before and
  74,560 B after (the table below). This is the *pipeline* cost the snapshot path pays, not the
  constructor's own copy, and the fast path moved it by zero bytes.

The existing, unmodified constructor was never doubling on the list and array sources every
production construction path actually passes.

**Root cause of the wrong prediction.** The C# compiler lowers a collection expression consisting
of a *single* spread element (`[.. elements]`, nothing else) targeting a `List<T>`-typed
destination directly to `new List<T>(elements)` — not an Add-per-element loop built from the
spread source's *static* type. `List<T>`'s own `IEnumerable<T>` constructor then does its own
*runtime* `is ICollection<T>` check: when the argument's actual type implements `ICollection<T>`
(every production `GrobArray` construction site passes a `List<GrobValue>` or a `GrobValue[]` — see
the site survey below), it reads `Count` and copies once via `CopyTo`; only a genuinely lazy,
non-`ICollection` source (verified separately with a hand-rolled `yield return` iterator: 49,432 B,
confirming the doubling growth path is real and reachable) falls back to incremental growth. That
path is reachable from a test — `RuntimeTypesTests` deliberately constructs from a LINQ `Select` —
but from no `src/` call site today. Both halves of the fast path are *current implementation
behaviour* of Roslyn and the BCL, not contracts either one guarantees, so this refutation is scoped
to today's toolchain and today's construction sources rather than asserted in general. D-386's
static-type reasoning was correct about the *parameter's* declared type but did not account for the
compiler's single-spread lowering or the BCL constructor's own internal fast path — the two
together already deliver exactly the pre-sizing D-386 proposed adding explicitly.

**No fix landed; the branch closes without one**, per this increment's own stop condition. The
explicit `ICollection<GrobValue>` switch was written, measured, confirmed redundant and reverted
— `src/Grob.Core/GrobArray.cs`'s constructor is unchanged from before this increment, now carrying
a short comment recording this finding so a future reader (or agent) does not re-propose the same
already-debunked branch.

**Construction-site survey (unchanged by this entry, recorded since it was the investigation's
main artefact).** Every `new GrobArray(...)` call in `src/` passing an existing collection was
enumerated and every one already benefits from the BCL fast path above: `VirtualMachine.cs`'s `NewArray`
opcode and the map `keys`/`values` properties (D-377) construct from a freshly-built
`GrobValue[]`; the `$snapshot` property (D-383) constructs from `GrobArray.Elements`, whose
runtime type is always `List<GrobValue>`; `ArrayNatives.Filter`/`Select`/`Sort` construct from a
`List<GrobValue>` or `GrobValue[]`; `StringMethodsPlugin`'s `string.split` constructs from a
`GrobValue[]` already built by an outer collection-expression spread. None mutates its source
during or after construction. Semantics (order, independence from source mutation, D-372's
shallow-copy element aliasing) were characterised with four new tests in
`tests/Grob.Core.Tests/RuntimeTypesTests.cs` — coverage this type did not have before, kept as the
increment's only landed change, since it fills a real gap regardless of the fix's fate.

**Measurements (local machine, not a canonical baseline — see D-387's own caveat on why; the same
`benchmark.yml`/`windows-latest` requirement applies).** `dotnet run -c Release --project
bench/Grob.Benchmarks -- --filter "*AttrSnapshotEmpty*" "*AttrBuild*" --job short` on the same
Intel Core i5-8400 machine as D-387, before and after applying (then reverting) the fast-path
branch:

| Benchmark | Before (unmodified) | After (explicit fast path) |
|---|---:|---:|
| `Run_AttrBuild` | 509,131 B/op (1,042,702,400 B / 2,048 ops) | 509,131 B/op (identical) |
| `Run_AttrSnapshotEmpty` | 583,692 B/op (597,700,128 B / 1,024 ops) | 583,692 B/op (1,195,400,256 B / 2,048 ops — identical) |
| Derived pure-snapshot cost | ≈74,560 B | ≈74,560 B (zero change) |

The short-run figures differ slightly from D-387's canonical-job numbers (509,131 B vs 508,316 B;
583,692 B vs 583,732 B; derived pure-snapshot cost 74,560 B vs D-387's committed 75,416 B) by
≈850 B of ordinary run-to-run variance between a short local job and D-387's canonical job on the
same machine, not by anything this entry changed — the before/after pair taken *on this branch* is
what matters, and it shows zero movement. **D-387's 75,416 B remains the figure of record**; this
entry's own 74,560 B is cited only to show its before/after pair, not as a competing measurement.

**The residual, reattributed.** The ≈75 KB pure-snapshot cost is **not** array-copy doubling — a
single isolated copy measures 24,080 B (above), so the residual is **≈3.1×** one copy. It is also
not the `for...in` loop's own iteration machinery: `attr-range` − `attr-empty` (D-387) measures an
*entire* compiled and executed 1,000-iteration range loop at 1,977 B, ≈2 B/iteration, while the
unattributed residual here is ≈50 B/iteration — **twenty-five times** that. An empty-bodied array
`for...in` lowers to an int counter, a comparison, a `GetIndex` returning a `GrobValue` struct and
a `SetLocal`, none of which allocates, so loop machinery cannot plausibly account for a ≈3.1×
multiple of a single copy. **The leading hypothesis is that the `for...in` snapshot path copies
more than once** — which would also explain why a constructor-level fix had no effect: fixing the
constructor's own pre-sizing does nothing if a second, unaccounted copy happens elsewhere on the
same path. This is unattributed and left for a future, separately measured increment; identifying
the second copy (or ruling it out) is not chased here, per this increment's explicit stop condition
on a refuted hypothesis.

**Why this still matters beyond a null result.** Phase 3b (D-385 Q2's per-category allocation
ceilings) was the reason D-313 wanted this checked before, not after, a threshold was set.
**Concretely: phase 3b must not derive a `Run_ArrayForIn` allocation ceiling until this residual is
attributed.** Setting one now would commit ≈50 KB per thousand-element `for...in` loop as expected,
gate-worthy behaviour; if the second-copy hypothesis above is later confirmed and fixed, removing
that cost would then mean *lowering* a published threshold — exactly the ratchet trap D-313
forbids in the other direction. This entry closes the doubling question so a ceiling is not derived
from a cost that does not exist, and opens the residual question so one is not derived from a cost
that might not need to exist either.

No opcode change. No new error code; count unchanged at **121**. Cites D-313 (the measurement
gate this satisfies), D-386 (the hypothesis this refutes), D-387 (the isolating measurement this
starts from), D-383 (the `for...in` contents-snapshot this investigates), D-372 (the shallow-copy
aliasing the characterisation tests protect) and `docs/design/bench-allocation-attribution.md` §5
(phase 1's original, unexplained figure).

### D-389 — Snapshot allocation residual attributed: not a second copy, a per-call `GetProperty` closure tax; three-copy hypothesis refuted; phase 3b unblocked (July 2026)

Area: VM — `GetProperty` dispatch / benchmarking attribution
Supersedes: none
Superseded by: none
Refines: D-388 (attributes the residual D-388 left open; closes its blocking condition)

**The residual is attributed, and the three-copy hypothesis D-388 proposed is refuted.**
Disassembling the minimal case (`xs := [1, 2, 3]; for x in xs { }`) and reading every
handler on the path confirms there is exactly **one** `new GrobArray(...)` call on the
array `for...in` path — the `$snapshot` `GetProperty` case (`VirtualMachine.cs:887`–890),
executed once regardless of array size or loop length. `GrobArray.Elements` returns the
live list directly (no defensive copy). The ≈75 KB residual is not a second or third
copy of the array's data — direct measurement (`GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread`,
D-388's own technique applied more narrowly, no BenchmarkDotNet) shows the residual is
**constant regardless of the snapshotted array's size** (48,072 B ± 160 B across array
sizes 3 through 5,000) and **identical for `"length"` and `"isEmpty"`**, an array
property read that never touches element data at all. A copy would scale with size;
this does not.

**Root cause: a C#-compiler closure-capture display-class allocation, paid on every
`GetProperty` dispatch against an array receiver, not gated by which branch of the case
actually runs.** `VirtualMachine.cs`'s `OpCode.GetProperty` case declares a closure at
:894–899 (`(callable, args) => InvokeCallable(callable, args, line, column, ct,
finallyContext)`, binding `ArrayNatives.GetMethod` for methods like `.append`) that
captures `line`/`column` (outer, per-dispatch-iteration-reassigned locals) alongside
locals declared in the same case body. The `"length"`/`"isEmpty"`/`"$snapshot"`
branches `break` out **before** that closure-declaring code, and by reading alone
should cost nothing beyond a struct push — but Roslyn allocates the display class
covering the shared lexical scope regardless of which sibling branch executes.
Confirmed mechanistically, not just measured, by an independent synthetic repro
carrying zero Grob code: a minimal C# method with the same shape (an early-return `if`
sibling, in one block, to a later lambda-declaring branch capturing an outer
per-iteration-reassigned local) reproduces the same "early-return branch still pays"
effect from C# semantics alone. This is a general `GetProperty`-on-array dispatch tax
— any user `.length`/`.isEmpty` read pays it, not only `for...in`'s internal emission.

**Reconciliation.** For the 1,000-element/1,000-iteration case: 24,080 B (the one
`$snapshot` copy, exactly D-388's isolated figure, confirmed unchanged when routed
through the real VM dispatch path) + 48,072 B (1,000 × the `GetProperty("length")`
closure tax the loop condition pays every iteration) + 96 B (`GetIndex`/`PopN` item
binding) + 344 B (bare loop arithmetic) = **72,592 B predicted, 72,592 B measured** —
exact, zero residual, for this entry's own isolated hand-assembled repro. The same
figure (72,536–72,596 B) reproduces via the real compiled `attr-build`-based fixtures,
measured directly rather than through BenchmarkDotNet. Against D-387's committed
75,416 B figure of record, ≈96–97% is accounted for by named site; the remaining ≈3–4%
(≈1,960–2,880 B) is left **unresolved** as a cross-harness difference — every figure
this entry produces comes from direct GC counters, every figure it is compared against
comes from BenchmarkDotNet. Harness/operation-batching overhead is the plausible account
(D-388 documented an ≈850 B gap of that kind between a short and a canonical local job),
but no matched-harness comparison was run, so the entry neither attributes the remainder
to harness overhead nor to an unidentified allocation site; settling it needs the same
fixture measured under both harnesses. Reported as an honest partial attribution rather
than folded into the headline result.

**Phase 3b is unblocked.** D-388's condition — the residual must be attributed before a
`Run_ArrayForIn` allocation ceiling is derived, so a later fix does not force lowering a
published threshold — is met: the residual is now named, sited and measured. A future
ceiling can be derived knowing it commits to (one D-383 copy) + (a per-call
`GetProperty` closure tax unrelated to array size), and knowing that removing the tax
component would _shrink_ a ceiling, the direction D-313's ratchet rule permits without
friction.

**No fix proposed or made** — this increment's explicit stop condition. The closure-tax
finding is left for a future, separately decided increment (candidate direction:
restructure `OpCode.GetProperty`'s case body so the closure-declaring statements are
scoped to their own block, narrowing the display class Roslyn generates — not designed
here). Full method, every measured table and the ablation/scaling/synthetic-repro
evidence trail: `docs/design/bench-snapshot-residual.md`. No `src/` change. No opcode
change. No new error code; count unchanged at **121**. Cites D-388 (the hypothesis
refuted and the blocking condition closed), D-387 (the figure of record and the
isolating technique refined here), D-386 (the original doubling hypothesis), D-383
(the contents-snapshot guarantee the one genuine copy implements), D-313 (the
measurement gate this satisfies) and `docs/design/bench-allocation-attribution.md`.

### D-390 — Benchmark baselines re-freeze on measurement-methodology change, unconditionally (August 2026)

Area: Tooling — benchmarking (gate policy)
Supersedes: none
Superseded by: none
Refines: D-313

**Decision.** Whenever a benchmark's *measurement methodology* changes — what region of
code is timed, what setup is hoisted out of the measured region, what invocation/unroll
strategy BenchmarkDotNet is forced into — as distinct from a change to the code under
test, the rolling and origin baselines for every benchmark that methodology touches are
re-frozen in the same change, unconditionally. The commit message and the decisions-log
entry record this explicitly as a **re-establishment** of the measurement basis, never
as a rebaseline absorbing a regression, because none occurred.

**Why this is a separate rule from D-313's ratchet trap, not a restatement of it.**
D-313 forbids updating a baseline to quietly absorb a real regression — a genuine
slowdown that happened and would otherwise compound invisibly sprint over sprint. This
rule addresses the opposite failure: a percentage comparison (per-sprint, cumulative) is
only meaningful when both sides measure the same thing, and a methodology change breaks
that precondition without the code under test changing at all. The two are easy to
conflate — both involve committing new baseline numbers — but the direction of harm
differs: skipping D-313's rule hides a real cost; skipping this one manufactures a fake
one.

**The triggering evidence.** The canonical `benchmark.yml` run `30707325720`
(2026-08-01, `windows-latest`, AMD EPYC 7763) compared against the still-committed
pre-rebuild `vm.json`/`vm.origin.json` (Intel Xeon Platinum 8370C, captured before
D-387's `vm` rebuild moved compilation into `[GlobalSetup]` and forced
`[IterationSetup]`'s `InvocationCount=1`/`UnrollFactor=1` — needed to keep each
iteration's fresh `VirtualMachine` isolated, which as a side effect removes
BenchmarkDotNet's normal operation-unrolling amortization). The raw per-sprint/cumulative
deltas: `Run_ControlFlow` **+343.8%** (61,174 ns → 271,508 ns), `Run_DeclAndArith`
**+147.6%** (12,224 ns → 30,263 ns), `Run_Interpolation` **+141.5%** (13,005 ns →
31,414 ns). None of these is a real VM or compiler slowdown — the old figures amortize
per-invocation overhead across an unrolled batch and include compilation; the new
figures measure one unamortized `vm.Run(chunk)` call with compilation already excluded.
Comparing them is comparing two different rulers, not two points on the same one.

**Why the build did not fail on this — a near-miss, not a working safeguard.** Two
independent, coincidental conditions suppressed these numbers from gating, neither of
which exists because of any mechanism protecting against a methodology change: `vm`'s
time axis is `Informational` under the §9.1 gating matrix (D-385/D-386 Q6) for an
unrelated reason (build-out sequencing, pending the full `endToEnd` corpus); and
separately, the fresh run's CPU (AMD EPYC 7763) does not match either baseline file's
CPU (Intel Xeon Platinum 8370C), which degrades the time comparison to informational
under D-333's `SameCpu` guard regardless of gating status. Had either condition been
otherwise — `vm` gating on time, or a CPU-matched canonical run — the identical
methodology change would have failed the build on a phantom regression, with nothing in
`BenchCheck`'s output pointing at "the measured region changed" as the cause; a
maintainer would read a red per-sprint or cumulative breach and start hunting for a
performance regression that was never there. `compile` is exactly this kind of category
today — time-gating, and its own cumulative axis is only informational because of the
separate, already-logged `compile.origin.json` CPU-placeholder gap (D-333, D-385 Q3),
not because of any protection against a methodology change. A future `compile`
methodology change landing on a CPU-matched run would hit this failure mode directly.

**Rejected.** Leaving this to reviewer judgement case-by-case — a passing build gives no
prompt to look, and a failing build points at the wrong cause, so the two moments a
reviewer would naturally check are exactly the moments this gap is invisible. A
`BenchCheck` mechanism to auto-detect a methodology change from the data — no field in a
BenchmarkDotNet report distinguishes "the code under test got slower" from "the harness
now measures a different region of code"; the two produce identical-shaped output. This
has to be a rule applied by whoever changes a benchmark class's
`[GlobalSetup]`/`[IterationSetup]`/measured-region shape, at the point they change it,
not something inferred after the fact.

**Cost.** None to any currently-committed baseline beyond what the phase-3b landing
entry (D-391, citing this one) applies immediately: `vm.json`/`vm.origin.json`
re-established from the `30707325720` canonical run under this rule, recorded there as a
re-establishment, not a rebaseline. No opcode change, no new error code; count unchanged
at **121**. Cites D-313 (the rule this sits beside, never inside), D-387 (the `vm`
rebuild whose methodology change surfaced this gap), D-333 (the CPU-identity guard whose
coincidental, unrelated application produced the near-miss), D-309 (`benchmark.yml`/
`windows-latest` as the canonical production path this rule governs).

### D-391 — Allocation ceilings: `lohTripwireBytes` renamed to a category/fixture-shaped total-allocation ceiling, derived from canonical figures (August 2026)

Area: Tooling — benchmarking (gate policy, implementation)
Supersedes: none
Superseded by: none
Refines: D-385 (Q2), D-387, D-390

**Phase 3b — completes D-385 Q2.** D-385 Q2 ratified redocumenting
`lohTripwireBytes` (85,000 B) as what it already functioned as — a total-per-operation
allocation ceiling compared against `Memory.BytesAllocatedPerOperation`, not an LOH
detector — and left deriving per-category or per-fixture-shape thresholds to phase 3.
This entry does that derivation, against the first canonical (`windows-latest`)
benchmark run since D-387's `vm`/`attribution` restructure landed: `30707325720`
(AMD EPYC 7763, .NET 10.0.10, 2026-08-01), dispatched against `origin/main` at `6f816d4`.

**The rename, mechanically.** `policy.json`'s single global `lohTripwireBytes` is
removed. `PolicyCategory` gains `AllocationCeilingBytes` (`double?`, the category's
default ceiling) and `BenchmarkAllocationCeilings` (`IReadOnlyDictionary<string, double>?`,
keyed by `BdnBenchmark.FullName`, taking precedence over the category default for the
benchmarks it names). No global fallback survives — the categories are provably
incommensurable, not merely differently sized: `vm` alone spans **441×** internally
(`Run_DeclAndArith` 2,344 B to `Run_MapForIn` 1,033,320 B), so a shared constant across
categories was never coherent and a shared default within `vm` is not much better.
`BenchCheck.BreachesLohTripwire(fresh, policy)` becomes
`BreachesAllocationCeiling(fresh, fullName, category)` — the benchmark's own
`BenchmarkAllocationCeilings` entry if present, else `category.AllocationCeilingBytes`;
absent both, the benchmark never breaches (the correct behaviour for `endToEnd`, which
has no ceiling configured while F8 leaves it empty — `Evaluate` already skips categories
with zero fresh benchmarks, so this is inert rather than a gap). `AllocClass
.LohTripwireBreach` renamed to `CeilingBreach`; both `Evaluate` call sites (the
fresh-only/`NewBenchmark` path and `ClassifyAlloc`) now thread the benchmark's `FullName`
and its `PolicyCategory` through instead of just `Policy`. `Cli.cs`'s per-row label moves
to `**allocation ceiling**`; the summary header's `LOH tripwire {N} B` clause is dropped
entirely rather than trying to enumerate every category's number inline — there is no
longer one figure that is true, and the per-row `Alloc status` column already carries a
breach. No `loh` naming survives in `tooling/Grob.BenchCheck`, `tooling/Grob.BenchCheck.Tests`
or `bench/Grob.Benchmarks/baseline/policy.json` — verified by a case-insensitive grep of
the tree, leaving only the historical prose in this log, in
`grob-benchmarking-strategy.md`'s own explanation of what changed, and unrelated genuine
CLR-LOH usage in `src/Grob.Vm/ValueStack.cs`/`ValueStackTests.cs` (the VM's own backing-array
sizing versus the real Large Object Heap threshold, D-332 — a different concern this
rename does not touch).

**Granularity — per-category default, per-benchmark override where the internal spread
demands it, following D-385 Q2's explicit "per-category (or per-fixture-shape)" clause
rather than one rigid taxonomy:**

- **`compile`** — one category default; both members (`Compile_TenPrints` 16,728 B,
  `Compile_TwoExpressions` 9,856 B) are the same shape and close in magnitude.
- **`vm`** — a scalar-dispatch default covering `Run_DeclAndArith`/`Run_Interpolation`/
  `Run_ControlFlow` (2,344–3,880 B, no collection snapshot), plus individual overrides for
  `Run_ArrayForIn` and `Run_MapForIn`. The two `for...in` fixtures are **not** folded into
  one shared for-in ceiling between them — they are themselves ~2× apart, and grouping
  them would reintroduce, one level down, the exact "one number spans too wide a range"
  problem this entry exists to fix.
- **`attribution`** — the same logic, not a category-wide ceiling from its largest member
  as first proposed. A single ceiling sized to `Run_AttrMapBuild` — 1,128,400 B, that
  fixture's 940,315 B measurement under this entry's 20% headroom convention — would let
  `Run_AttrEmpty` (42,849 B) grow **26×** unnoticed (the multiple is ceiling-to-measured,
  1,128,400 / 42,849; measured-to-measured is ~22×), and "`compile` already covers that
  shape" does not hold: `attr-empty` measures the whole pipeline *plus* `VirtualMachine`
  construction *plus* plugin registration, so a regression in either of the latter two
  lands here and in nothing `compile` watches — and it is the fixture every other `attr-*`
  subtraction treats as a stable floor (D-387), so it needs its own live protection, not a
  borrowed one. `Run_AttrEmpty`/`Run_AttrRange` (42,849 B/46,145 B) share a floor-shape
  default; `Run_AttrNative`, `Run_AttrArrayDispatch`, `Run_AttrBuild`,
  `Run_AttrSnapshotEmpty` and `Run_AttrMapBuild` (232,239 B–940,315 B, a ~4× internal
  spread) each get their own override.
- **`endToEnd`** — no ceiling configured; F8 is open, zero fresh benchmarks exist to
  derive one from.

**Headroom — one convention, stated once, applied uniformly:**
`round_to_nearest_100(1.20 × canonical measured value)`. 20% is double the existing
`allocPercent` (10%, the per-sprint *relative* growth gate that already tracks
incremental creep) — sized larger because this ceiling is the coarse, rare-firing
absolute backstop, not the primary signal, but still tight enough that nothing short of
roughly doubling slips through silently.

| Category / benchmark | Measured (canonical) | Ceiling | Basis |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `compile` (default) | 16,728 B | **20,100 B** | `Compile_TenPrints` |
| `vm` scalar default | 3,880 B | **4,700 B** | `Run_Interpolation` |
| `vm` → `Run_ArrayForIn` | 531,616 B | **637,900 B** | itself |
| `vm` → `Run_MapForIn` | 1,033,320 B | **1,240,000 B** | itself |
| `attribution` floor default | 46,145 B | **55,400 B** | `Run_AttrRange` |
| `attribution` → `Run_AttrNative` | 232,239 B | **278,700 B** | itself |
| `attribution` → `Run_AttrArrayDispatch` | 460,101 B | **552,100 B** | itself |
| `attribution` → `Run_AttrBuild` | 509,095 B | **610,900 B** | itself |
| `attribution` → `Run_AttrSnapshotEmpty` | 583,609 B | **700,300 B** | itself |
| `attribution` → `Run_AttrMapBuild` | 940,315 B | **1,128,400 B** | itself |

**Three of these ten sit _below_ the old 85,000 B constant — `compile` 20,100 B, `vm`
scalar 4,700 B and `attribution` floor 55,400 B — and the other seven sit above it.**
This entry therefore does not leave every threshold where it was or tighter: it replaces
a misapplied global limit with shape-specific ceilings, tightening those three shapes and
raising the permitted figure for the seven larger ones. That is the intended outcome and
it is stated plainly rather than framed as "nothing is loosened", which the table above
would contradict.

What justifies the seven. The old number was never derived from any of these fixtures'
legitimate allocation — it was borrowed from an unrelated CLR concept and compared
against the wrong quantity from the start (D-385 Q2) — and every one of those seven
fixtures already measured above it, so for them it was never a threshold they were
passing and never a protection the new figure removes. Setting a first threshold for a
correctly-named mechanism against a newly-correct, newly-canonical measurement is the
substance of the change; the three shapes whose ceilings fall below 85,000 B are gated
more tightly than they have ever been. What would now trigger a failure that does not
today: any of the ten figures above growing by more than its stated 20% headroom, on any
category regardless of its `gating` flag. The two `vm` `for...in` ceilings **include an
≈48 B/call `GetProperty` closure-capture tax** D-389 attributed (per-iteration,
independent of array/map size). Per D-313's ratchet rule, a future fix to that tax must
**lower** these ceilings, never justify raising them — recorded here so that fix, when it
lands, is measured against this entry rather than treated as licence to hold the ceiling
where it is.

**The revision rule.** A ceiling is legitimately raised for a new benchmark of a
genuinely different allocation shape, or a deliberate feature landing with measured,
accepted cost — always as a stated, logged decision citing the new measurement, following
this same 20%-headroom convention. It is not legitimately raised to silently absorb an
unexplained regression — D-313's ratchet trap, restated at the ceiling's own granularity.
A ceiling may be lowered freely once a component contributing to it (the `GetProperty` tax
above, say) is fixed; the ratchet only forbids motion in the direction that hides cost.

**Canonical derivations the run also supplied**, closing the gap D-387 left open pending
`attr-array-dispatch`'s canonical capture (D-387: "its number is not yet measured"):
Stdlib native cost **186.1 B/call** ((`attr-native` − `attr-range`) ÷ 1000); array-member
dispatch cost **414.0 B/call** ((`attr-array-dispatch` − `attr-range`) ÷ 1000) — a
**227.9 B/call** dispatch tax over the Stdlib path; array growth (1,000 appends)
**48,994 B** (`attr-build` − `attr-array-dispatch`); pure contents-snapshot cost
**74,514 B** (`attr-snapshot-empty` − `attr-build`). All four reproduce phase 1/D-387's
local-machine figures within measurement noise, now on canonical hardware.

**`vm.json`/`vm.origin.json` re-established, `attribution.json`/`attribution.origin.json`
committed for the first time.** Per **D-390** (logged separately in this session, since
the rule is general and not specific to this increment): D-387's `vm` rebuild changed both
*what* is measured (execution alone, compilation excluded) and *how* (`[IterationSetup]`
forcing `InvocationCount=1`/`UnrollFactor=1`, removing BenchmarkDotNet's amortization) —
the still-committed pre-rebuild files produced raw deltas of
+343.8%/+147.6%/+141.5% against the canonical run that were never real regressions
(D-390's full analysis, including why the build did not fail on them). Both files are
replaced from `30707325720`, recorded as a re-establishment, not a rebaseline.
`attribution.json`/`attribution.origin.json` are a genuine first measurement — the
category has never had a committed baseline.

**Proof the ceiling still fires, not merely present.** Re-ran `BenchCheck` against the
canonical artifacts with `Run_ArrayForIn`'s reported allocation deliberately inflated to
700,000 B — above its 637,900 B override, comfortably under the 4,700 B scalar default it
would otherwise fall back to were the override absent. Result: `Outcome.Regression`,
`**allocation ceiling**` on that row alone, every other row (including `Run_MapForIn`,
untouched) reading `info`/`ok` exactly as the unmodified run does. The gate is
demonstrably live, not quietly always-pass.

**`grob-benchmarking-strategy.md`.** §8's `policy.json` shape example — three categories,
missing `attribution` since D-387 added it without updating this example — folded into
the same edit as the rename; the §8 baseline-file list and the "`vm.json` describes a
stale measurement" note updated to record the re-establishment instead. New **§9.2**
documents the mechanism in full: what it was and why that stopped working, the rename,
the granularity rationale per category, the headroom convention, the full ceiling table
with derivations, and the revision rule — so the documented gate and the enforced gate
stay the same thing (the ADR-0018 precedent D-385 Q3/Q6 already applied to this corpus).
§9's Axis 3 prose and §9.1's gating-matrix column header renamed from "LOH tripwire" to
"Allocation ceiling"; §9.1's `endToEnd` row states "Not configured" rather than
implying a number exists.

**Tests.** `BenchCheckTests.cs`: `PolicyWith`'s `lohTripwireBytes` parameter renamed to
`allocationCeilingBytes`; the two existing tripwire-behaviour tests renamed and updated
for `CeilingBreach`/`BreachesAllocationCeiling`; four new cases prove the restructured
mechanism live — a per-benchmark override passing when under it, the same override still
firing on a deliberately inflated value, the category default governing a benchmark with
no override of its own, and a category with no ceiling configured never breaching however
large the reported allocation. `CliRenderTests.cs`: the `LohTripwireBreach` theory case
and its render-label assertion renamed; the culture-invariance test — previously anchored
on the now-removed global header figure — re-anchored on the per-row `Alloc` column's
byte formatting instead, preserving the same de-DE-locale regression coverage. Full
solution (`Grob.slnx`) builds and tests clean, all `dotnet test` runs across every project
passing.

No opcode change. No new error code; count unchanged at **121**. Cites D-385 (Q2, the
decision this completes), D-386, D-387 (the restructure whose canonical figures this
derives every threshold from, and whose pending `attr-array-dispatch` measurement this
closes), D-388, D-389 (the residual attribution and the removable tax component the
`vm` `for...in` ceilings commit to), D-390 (the re-establishment rule this applies to
`vm`'s baselines), D-333, D-313, D-309, `docs/design/bench-allocation-attribution.md` and
`docs/design/bench-snapshot-residual.md` (both findings notes, cited throughout for
figures this entry did not itself re-measure).

### D-392 — PR #174 review follow-ups: D-390's near-miss analysis corrected; a deferred allocation-ceiling reporting enhancement noted (August 2026)

Area: Tooling — benchmarking (gate policy, correction)
Supersedes: none
Superseded by: none
Refines: D-390

**D-390's near-miss analysis is corrected — D-390's own entry is not edited, per this
corpus's standing rule that a prior entry is never rewritten (the D-385/D-386 precedent:
"D-313's own entry is never edited").**

D-390 states that two coincidental, unrelated conditions — `vm`'s time axis already
being `Informational` under the §9.1 gating matrix, and the fresh run's CPU not
matching either baseline's — together suppressed three phantom time-axis regressions
(`Run_ControlFlow` +343.8%, `Run_DeclAndArith` +147.6%, `Run_Interpolation` +141.5%)
from failing the canonical run `30707325720`, and frames this as a near-miss: a build
that passed only by coincidence. **The canonical run's regression gate did not pass.**
Verified directly against the job's own log (`gh run view 30707325720 --job=91388583779`,
re-confirmed via the Actions API's `jobs[].steps[].conclusion` field): the "Check
regression gate" step's `conclusion` is `failure`, the step output reads
`## Benchmark regression gate — REGRESSION`, and the job exits `Process completed with
exit code 1`. Under the policy committed at the time of that run — `policy.json`'s
still-global `lohTripwireBytes: 85000`, unrenamed and unrestructured until D-391 —
both `vm` `for...in` benchmarks breached it outright: `| vm | Run_ArrayForIn | — | — |
new | — | 531,616 B | **LOH tripwire** |` and `| vm | Run_MapForIn | — | — | new | —
| 1,033,320 B | **LOH tripwire** |`. Both rows classify `NewBenchmark` on the time
axis (the pre-rebuild `vm.json` carried no entries for either fixture) but the tripwire
is unconditional regardless of that classification or of a category's `gating` flag
(D-333; `BenchCheck.Evaluate`'s fresh-only path applies `BreachesLohTripwire` before
falling back to `NewBenchmark`) — exactly the D-332-class defect the mechanism exists
to catch, working as designed, on this run.

**D-390's analysis is therefore incomplete, not merely imprecise: it answers "why did
the time axis not fail" for a run whose own conclusion the entry never checked, and
that conclusion was failure.** The two time-axis guards it names are real and correctly
described — they did suppress those three numbers from being *counted* toward the
outcome — but the entry's framing ("why the build did not fail... a near-miss, not a
working safeguard") asserts a fact about the run, not only about the mechanism, and
that factual claim is wrong.

**The standing rule D-390 exists to state is unaffected — strengthened, not
weakened.** Re-freezing rolling and origin baselines unconditionally on a
measurement-methodology change does not depend on whether the illustrative run passed
or failed; it depends on a percentage comparison being invalid the moment the ruler
changes, independent of outcome. What changes is the *illustration* of the danger:
this run did not silently pass with a hidden time-axis problem — it loudly failed for
an entirely unrelated, correct reason (the allocation-ceiling mismeasurement D-391
fixes), and that failure gave a reader no occasion to ever notice the time-axis
figures were comparing two different rulers. A maintainer diagnosing this run's actual
failure would reasonably conclude "the allocation ceiling is too tight for legitimate
`for...in` cost" — correct — and stop there, never discovering the methodology
problem underneath. **Three independent coincidences masking a genuine methodology
change from ever surfacing as the visible reason for a red build is a better argument
for unconditional re-freezing than two** — the mechanism that did catch a problem on
this run caught a different one, by chance, and could easily not have (a hypothetical
run where allocation was already within the old tripwire's headroom, or where the
`vm` category's allocation percentage-vs-baseline axis were gating, would have passed
outright with the time-axis methodology error fully live and undetected).

**Also recorded here, not built in this PR:** PR #174's review (CodeRabbit) proposed
carrying the applied allocation ceiling on `BenchmarkDelta` so a `CeilingBreach` row
names which threshold it broke — the category default or a specific per-benchmark
override. This is a genuine diagnostic gap opened by D-391's own per-benchmark
overrides: "ceiling breach" alone no longer says which of, for example, `vm`'s 4,700 B
scalar default or `Run_ArrayForIn`'s 637,900 B override actually fired. Deliberately
scoped out of the rename-and-derive-thresholds PR it surfaced in — the touch points
are a new `BenchmarkDelta` field, the three `Evaluate` construction sites that build
one, and a `Cli.Render` change — and left for its own small, separately reviewed
increment. This entry is the durable pointer to that follow-up beyond the PR's own
comment thread.

No opcode change. No new error code; count unchanged at **121**. Cites D-390
(corrected, not edited), D-391 (the increment whose review produced both findings
here), D-333 (the tripwire's unconditional-regardless-of-`NewBenchmark`-or-`gating`
behaviour, the mechanism this correction turns on), and PR #174.
